utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this next witness, as far as I can see, it's Mr. Colm Doyle. I believe that it is unacceptable to even in part treat him under Rule 92 bis or to shorten his testimony. He was the chief of the observer mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, of the monitoring mission in the critical time. He talks about very important facts from that period; peace plans, the referendum. He attended meetings of the National Assembly, and so on. So I believe that it is completely unacceptable for him to be shortened in any way by using this usual practice of 92 bis, and I am categorically opposed to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be borne in mind when it comes to considering the time for cross-examination that there have been parts which the Trial Chamber has ordered should be dealt with under that Rule. They are not the significance parts of the evidence. The significance parts of the evidence will be given live, but we shall, as I say, in determining how long you have for cross-examination, allow you to have longer because of that reason, longer than the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was no translation at all from English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, may I address you on another matter, in private session, for about one minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there translation? Mr. Tapuskovic has the channel. Yes, Mr. Nice. I think there's a problem about the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I address you for one minute in private session about an unrelated matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber has an exhibit bundle of some 29 or -- 29 tabs, although it will not be necessary to go beyond number 19, the remainder being intercepts, the -- which he is going to be able to authenticate without producing in a more detailed way. The tabs are not entirely chronological because the first 12, I think it is, are the annexes to his statement which has been in part 92 bis'd, and it seemed more sensible to stick to the order of those original annexures and therefore the other exhibits he'll be producing follow on from tab 12, as I say I think it is. May that exhibit be given a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the binder for the exhibits for Mr. Doyle will be Prosecution Exhibit 515.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust the Chamber has the witness summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Colm Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you a colonel in the Irish defence forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, you made a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. Did you go through an exercise with an officer of the court attesting to the accuracy of that statement subject to one or two very minor changes?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that statement can be found at tab 1 of Exhibit 515, with the minor corrections at an early part of that tab. And the Court having allowed part of the witness's evidence to be taken under the process of 92 bis as read, I'll deal with the balance viva voce in the standard way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, were you seconded or whatever from the Irish defence forces in 1991 to the European Community Monitoring Mission ECMM?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with your arrival in Sarajevo, as you were deployed elsewhere to begin with, I think; dealing with your arrival in Sarajevo, did you arrive there on the 24th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I went to Sarajevo on the 24th of November, 1991 to take over as head of the monitoring mission for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you based then at the Hotel Bosna in Ilidza, a residential suburb of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour will see we've got a map of Sarajevo available. It may be it's a map that will be of value to the Court, we'll wait and see, with other Sarajevo witnesses. Can it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Prosecution Exhibit 343, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I shan't actually be asking Colonel Doyle to deal with very many features of the map and it may be the Court will already be familiar with the general shape of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, you had been to Sarajevo before, I think for three days on the 11th of October; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Sarajevo for approximately three days before I was deployed to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On arrival on the 24th of November, what if anything did you notice or sense about the state of conflict in the area?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, because I had been in the area of operations, as we refer to it, for some time, there was a feeling that the situation was beginning to get rather tense, and there was some concern being expressed about the consequences of the withdrawal of the federal army, the JNA, from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Amongst your duties as head of mission, were you obliged to liaise with other monitoring teams situated in Bihac, Banja Luka, Tuzla, Mostar, as well as in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. Part of our function was to deploy monitor teams to the various locations covering the ethnic groups in Bosnia. So we picked those as an indication where we would get the best sort of information as to the developing situation within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, as the Chamber already knows, ECMM monitors were drawn from a wide range of countries. And I think that the monitoring team sent nightly reports, and one of your operations officers - this is paragraph 4 - would do a combined report collating all the relevant material; correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then that report was sent either by you or by someone in your team to the head of the ECMM in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your particular duty - paragraph 5 - given your role as head of the mission, to maintain contact with the civilian and political leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, where the teams would have contact in the localities where they were deployed. When I took over as head of the mission, I was asked to remain in contact with the party leaderships.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Following your deployment on the 24th, then, to this particular position, a first or an early meeting of significance was on the 27th of November when you spoke to the Bosnian Prime Minister Jure Pelivan?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have your summary there and I forecast the Chamber may not object to your looking at it. I think you also have diaries.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have diaries of where I went and who I met on the various dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But so far as possible, Colonel, if you can speak from recollection on matters of importance, assisted as you will be by documents that we'll be looking at, that will probably be the preferred course of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the witness could have a binder of exhibits. Is there a spare one for the usher to display on the overhead projector or not? If there's one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it may be, Colonel Doyle, if you'd like to turn, in the binder that's going to come your way, to tab 15. And if the usher would be good enough, when possible, to display the relevant tabs on the overhead projector because I'm afraid we haven't got this material on Sanction yet. Just tell us, please, very briefly about your meeting with the Prime Minister on the 27th of November.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: One of the first requests that was made of me when I became head of the mission was that the Prime Minister, Mr. Pelivan, asked to meet with me in his office, and as well as welcoming me into the appointment, he wanted to bring to my attention some of the concerns that had been expressed by his office, particularly in relation to the fact that the JNA had been accused of taking in armaments in the form of rockets in a civilian four-truck convoy from Montenegro. These rockets had been confiscated by the civilian police, and the Prime Minister informed me that the JNA had intimated to him that if he didn't hand over these weapons, that they would have to take action. I suggested to the Prime Minister that it might be of benefit were he to open up dialogue with the federal army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We see that reflected in tab 15, paragraph A, where there's a reference to a feeling, in the middle of the paragraph, that the build-up by the JNA is a threat to the stability of the country, and that relates to the continuous withdrawal of JNA units and equipment from Croatia leading to a build-up in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Paragraph B deals with the four civilian trucks carrying approximately a hundred tons of rockets. C, to the JNA's being subject of a government request for full cooperation. And then D in your report on this meeting, you deal with the economic stagnation caused by blockades of roads and bridges, further damaged by the decision of Serbia to halt food exports to other republics, as announced. This is seen as a further Serbian attempt to weaken Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then you make this point: Should this decision persist, the government may be forced to look to the Orient and Muslim-friendly countries for trade assistance. Was that something that was covered by the Prime Minister, or was that something that was your own interpretation or calculation of future events?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, the Prime Minister intimated that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well. Paragraph 7 of the summary: On the 6th of December, did you travel to Trebinje and, in accordance with your normal practice, meet the mayor?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think he was a former truck driver working in Dubrovnik. What, if anything, did you observe - again from memory or from notes - as to his attitude, and what concerns did that give you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was struck by the fact that this gentleman was in uniform, which is the first time I'd met the mayor of a location who wore a uniform, and some of the expressions he had I found to be very radical. He spoke about the return of the Third Reich, he talked about his opposition to -- he mentioned the Jews. He mentioned the Vatican. And I was very concerned and quite surprised that a man who appeared to me to be quite radical was holding the position of mayor of a town in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, of course, an early or comparatively early stage still of your general familiarisation with your job as head --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were getting the sense of the location. And I think on that same day you met General Strugar, or Lieutenant General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I met him with my senior operations officer and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to your account of what happened, I think you have with you - we needn't produce it - a photograph of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which has an annotation on the back which you've recently looked at and which has reminded you of a detail not in your statement and not in the summary. With that in mind, and you can tell us about the photograph if necessary, tell us about the meeting with him. Where was -- where was the meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I know that I left Trebinje. It was in some location not too far from Trebinje, and I think it might have been his field headquarters. And when we were met, I was informed that the general was not immediately available to meet with me because he was dealing with a problem which arose, and I intimated that if he couldn't see me, then there was no use in me remaining. So about five minutes later I was told that he would meet with me and we then met for about 25 minutes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you notice about his tone and so on?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: General Strugar was very perturbed and there had been a flurry of activity going on with people coming in and out which I wasn't too clear about. He then opened up the dialogue by telling me that he was -- had been very busy that period of time that I arrived but he felt obliged to meet with me. He also mentioned to me that because there were paramilitary troops -- he intimated there were Croats who had fired on his troops, he had no option but to take retaliatory action, and he admitted to me that he had fired on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, he said that these were paramilitaries, or implied or indicated that they were paramilitaries and Croats. Did he say where they were that they were firing on his troops?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, he didn't say where they -- I assumed that they were troops that had come in from Croatian or were on the territory of Bosnia in Western Herzegovina, but I didn't know or did he say to me where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By that stage, had you ever been to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, have you ever been to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have never been to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So its precise topography and so on is unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he seek to justify the attack he was acknowledging on Dubrovnik by reference to these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, in the sense he intimated to me, as far as I recall, that he was not going to tolerate people interfering and killing his troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he give you any details of killings or numbers of killings or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No. He didn't say to me how many had been killed, but certainly he did admit to me that he was obliged to take retaliatory action and that he had taken action against the city of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your annotated photograph reminds you of what? Just explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I took a lot of photographs because of historical record out there, and I asked the general would he mind standing in for a photograph with myself and my operations officer. He conceded to do that. It was my tendency then that when I got some of these photographs, I would notate on the back what they refer to, and the notation on the back of that photograph which I made after it was developed was that it gave the date, which was the 6th of December, 1991, and it was with General Strugar the day he launched an artillery attack on Dubrovnik, killing 16 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that detail, the killing of 16 people, was available to you then even if you can't track its source now?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have no recollection of why I mentioned that figure but I know it's actually notated on the back of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you met Strugar once again in February, 1992, in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I met him with the then head of the monitor mission, Ambassador Cutileiro, for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked if you noticed anything about his rank at that stage, whether it was up or down, and the answer is you don't know.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on from December 1991 to January 1992, on the 28th of January of 1992, did you have your first meeting with Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where and in what setting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the office, as far as I recall, of Mrs. Plavsic, who was one of the Serb members of the Bosnian Presidency, and the meeting was held at my instigation in order to meet with the party political leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this was in which town?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: This was in the city of Sarajevo. In the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, as you're going to tell us, I think, your contacts tended to be or were focused on the Presidency itself at that time.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. Almost all of the -- all of the politicians I met with, the party political leaders, and a lot of the meetings were held in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For a short period of time it being possible to meet different groups together, later on having to deal with them all separately. Would that be a correct summary of your position?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your impression of Karadzic and his approach?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, Radovan Karadzic was very pleased to me with me on that occasion. I remember him expressing his gratitude that as head of the monitor mission I would give time to meeting with him. He -- my view was very clearly the leader of the SDS party. He was very concerned to get the message across that he was very supportive of what the monitor mission was trying to achieve and that he felt that having dialogue on a regular basis would the leadership of the SDS would be good for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had subsequent meetings with him and with other members of the SDS leadership. Can you give the Judges any indication of the sort of frequency or number of meetings that you had or would that be unrealistic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't recall how many official meetings I would have had when I was head of the monitor mission, but as the situation developed, I met with him more frequently. And also when the head of the monitor mission from Zagreb came to the city, we had meetings with the Serb leadership which would have included Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, and the third member was mainly Krajisnik who was the president, I understand, of the Parliament. I also met, on occasions, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, with the benefit of those encounters, were you able to form a view as to who did what, who called the shots, who deferred to whom?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the one person who didn't speak any English was Mr. Krajisnik; however, I knew that Dr. Karadzic conferred with him considerably. But all of them, I felt, deferred to Radovan Karadzic, so it would have been my distinct impression that he was the -- he was undoubtedly and indisputably the leader of the Bosnian Serbs and they all deferred to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Krajisnik, when he spoke, did he speak through interpreters or how? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Most of the time that I had meetings with him, he spoke in English himself. There would also be -- their own interpreter would be there in case of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, Krajisnik you say spoke in English?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No. Krajisnik did not speak any English certainly that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So he spoke through interpreters or through someone else?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: He spoke through an interpreter, or else he would speak directly to Dr. Karadzic and he in turn then would speak in English. Nikola Koljevic was a good speaker of English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 13th and 14th of February, was there the start of a round of conferences on the future of Bosnia and did that happen in Villa Konak in Sarajevo under the chairmanship of Ambassador Jose Cutileiro from Portugal?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your role in all of this?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My role at the time was I was requested by the -- this delegation who were part of the Conference on Yugoslavia to clarify the various positions in Sarajevo. So it became the practice for me to give a briefing to these people when they came to Sarajevo, to bring them up-to-date on the developments within the political and military situation. I was also asked if I would be available on a sort of a standby so that during talks with the political leaders, of which I did not play any part, but I would be readily available in case these negotiators would look for my service or for my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And without being subject to any false modesty but just telling it as it is, how were your briefings valued, as you understood it, by people, for example, like Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, Lord Carrington did say to me on the first occasion I met with him, he asked me what I -- he inferred to me that he had been nearly three days in Sarajevo and that he had spoken to all sides, and one side would counter what the other side had said. So my name was given to him, I understand, by the Presidency as somebody who would probably have a neutral and impartial view of what was going on, particularly as I had teams deployed throughout the republic. So he asked if I would go with him in his car to the airport because he was about to leave, which I did, and I gave him a general briefing in the car, and his remark when he left the car was that he had learned more from me in 15 minutes than he had learned in the previous three days. So I did get the impression that he was appreciative of my knowledge of the situation as an impartial observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he express to you any view on the ease or difficulty in obtaining a truthful account from others?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I know that he did mention on one occasion that all the parties lied and that it was very difficult to get at the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on then from that first round of the conference, on the 27th of February, did you have a meeting with the Bosnian Serb Information Minister, Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It touched on the television station. A brief account of that, please, and its significance as you saw it in your position.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The Minister for Information Ostojic asked to meet me. He made a request that I would go to his office, which I did. I was very surprised that he asked if I could use my influence in persuading the Minister of the Interior to give him, that is Mr. Ostojic, more responsibility for communications within the country. What he was referring to here was his objection that the Minister for Information -- I beg your pardon, that the Minister of the Interior had control over Sarajevo television and not he as Minister for Information. I was very surprised that the head of the monitor mission was being asked to get involved in what was essentially an inter-Minister dispute of the government of Bosnia. So I told him that I would attempt to meet with the Minister of the Interior to get his side of the argument. Over the next I think maybe two days, I met with the Deputy Minister of the Interior who informed me that it was not any concern of Mr. Ostojic, he had no responsibility for Sarajevo television and that's the way it would remain, and he gave me the opinion that all Mr. Ostojic wanted was actual control of the television station itself. So I felt it was not something that the monitor mission should get involved in and I informed both sides that I was no longer taking up this issue on anybody's behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the effort to obtain control of the television station through you an indication of how things were in the city and the state generally.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that there was certainly a division within the government, depending on what side you came from, and that there were difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The referendum on independence took place on the 29th of February of 1992. Your involvement in that was anything in relation to the referendum itself or the voting or did you stick out -- stay out of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was asked by the head of the mission in Zagreb to attend the parliamentary debate on the question of whether a referendum should be held in Bosnia to determine independence and sovereignty. I attended the referendum which lasted for about maybe 36 hours. I had an interpreter with me. I was welcomed into the Chamber by the -- by the President, and I stayed there for the parliamentary debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ambassador Cutileiro, I think, had asked you to approach the party leaders?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, Ambassador Cutileiro asked me if I would contact the party leaders and ask them what they felt would be the outcome were Bosnia to be given its independence. I spoke with the president, and he told me that although the Serbs would not be very happy if Bosnia became independent, that they in time would come round to accepting it. I then asked the leader --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By "the president," you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic. I then asked, sometime later, Radovan Karadzic what he felt would happen if Bosnia was given its independence and he said that there would be conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "conflict," can you remember the terminology he used?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I had the distinct impression he was referring to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, the results of that referendum - paragraph 17 - were announced on what day? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I think they were announced on the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think it was a formal press conference dealing with that. You returned to your headquarters. Now, I don't know how comfortable you are with just simply pointing things out on the map, and I don't know to what extent the learned Judges from this or other cases are familiar with Sarajevo, but you've been provided with a pointer, and it may help if you can just, looking at that exhibit, which is 343, tab 7, just start the process of familiarisation if the Judges require it. The old town is where?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The old town is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And the big main street --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: This is the airport here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The big main street with high-rise buildings on certainly one side, it runs right the way through it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Along here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you're --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was out on this side, and Ilidza --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over there on the west.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The west.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that map occasionally, I think. You were dressed, I think, in civilian clothes for a particular reason.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: When the results of the referendum were announced at a press conference, I was asked if I would attend. I said yes, but I attended in civilian clothes rather than in the white uniforms we wore as members of the monitor mission. I did this because before, when the Bosnian Serbs wanted hold their referendum, Radovan Karadzic asked, or invited the monitor mission to -- to monitor, I suppose, the holding of the Serb referendum and I felt that was not appropriate, so I declined. Therefore, I felt that if I was going to be appearing at the press conference for the referendum in general that was being announced by the Prime Minister, that it might be appropriate if I didn't attend that as a member of the monitor mission, so I decided to wear a suit rather than to wear the white uniform of the monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you got back to your base at Ilidza, but what did you discover the following morning?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The following morning a member of the hotel staff came to me and he brought me out to the window, and he said, Do you notice anything? And I said no. And he said there's nobody moving. Now, at that time in the mornings all of the students, we used to see them quite frequently, and then he told me that the city was blockaded. This is the first information I had that blockades had been erected in the city. I was also informed by my operations officer that some of my monitors who were in the city the previous evening could not get back to the hotel. I viewed this as quite serious, and I then made contact with the Presidency to ascertain what was happening, and then I was informed as to the nature of the blockades and why the blockades had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by whom had they been set up and for what apparent purpose?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the information I had at the time was that they were set up as a result of the killing of a Serb at a wedding the previous day and tensions were high. However, I was informed by various parties that the reason they had been erected was that the Serbs were objecting to the principle of the referendum and the referendum results. And I was also concerned that I had been informed that there might be a difficulty in arranging for the departure of the referendum -- the civilian referendum observers from countries of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you in the early afternoon drive to the city centre with your operations officer? And of course, as the Judges will already remember, the ECMM is entirely an unarmed mission.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I went into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as you could judge, how necessary would it have been for the blockades you then saw to have been planned in advance?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I suppose my military training would lead me to believe that these barricades went up very, very quickly. They seemed to go up in the all the strategic positions around the city, and it would be my view that they had already been planned in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your way in, was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Near the Bristol Hotel, which is on the main route into the city, our -- we came across a barricade, and very close to the barricade there was a considerable amount of shooting going on. Shots were being fired at people on the barricade from a building on the left-hand side. I was very concerned for my own safety and that of my officer and driver, so I was about to withdraw when a red car -- a Red Cross car came with a flag flying and passed by my car and somebody inside indicated that I should follow. And when we approached the barricade, the barricade was lifted to allow me through. I suppose the main reason for this was that my car was easily recognisable; it had the motif of the monitor mission and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were now in your white uniform?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was now in my white uniform, on official duty. So I was facilitated with passage through the barricade and made my way to the -- to the Holiday Inn where all activity seemed to be centred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You there met Mr. Ganic, the deputy president of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I met Mr. Ganic, who was at that time head of the Crisis Committee, and we had a discussion about what action should be taken to defuse the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you saw Karadzic there as well that day at some stage?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Dr. Karadzic later on. I had been informed on my arrival that he was ensconced in a floor of the hotel with his Crisis Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You reported on this -- and this is one of the original annexures to the witness's statement so it's early on in the tabs. It's tab 6, originally annex 5 to the witness statement. We're not going to go through your earlier reports, Colonel Doyle, because they're produced by your witness statement which is admitted under the provisions of the Tribunal called 92 bis, but I think if the Judges do find themselves going through it, they'll see that your earlier reports were handwritten at some stages when you were right at the beginning of your mission. By this stage you've got proper equipment?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this report sets out what?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: This was a report that I submitted to the head of the mission, and it set out the official SDS demands that were handed to me in the Holiday Inn and for which I discussed Mr. Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can see those demands: Activities relating to international recognition to be stopped, conference to be continued, media to stop reporting, Bosnia-Herzegovina is already recognised. Then reference to the political situation and assassins to be caught, Yutel TV to be discontinued and a division of television and radio into ethnic channels. Further down, we see Ganic accepted the responsibility to secure the departure of the European observers. Then over the page, at 1700 hours Ostojic, senior observer of the European parliament, HRC, and his officers were permitted to approach one of the barricades. It became apparent that the armed Serbs would only consider dismantling the barricades on the directive of the SDS leadership. Can you just explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I decided after I'd spoken to Mr. Ganic that I would try and use my position to make an approach to one of the barricades to see if I could defuse the situation. So I approached a barricade that was on a bridge behind the parliamentary building. I was with Dr. Ostojic and, as you say, the chairman of the monitoring group, and I was easily recognisable, and one of the personnel on the barricade gave me permission to walk across the bridge, which I did. And then through the interpreter I asked if they would consider dismantling the barricade because I had been in contact with the Crisis Committee of the SDS and had dealt with Dr. Ganic -- or Mr. Ganic. The person I spoke to on the barricade inferred that the only condition in which he would dismantle the barricade would be on the word of Dr. Radovan Karadzic. I withdrew at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I think you had some dealings at this stage with Lieutenant Colonel Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dimitrijevic was a JNA officer with the rank of lieutenant colonel who was given as a sort a liaison officer to the monitor mission. And when the decision was made to move the referendum observers back to the airport, I was very well aware of the fact that we would have to go through a considerable amount of barricades and the situation was very tense and very dangerous, so I requested of this lieutenant colonel if he would accompany me and permission was granted for that to be done. The JNA provided, I think it were, two coaches, and we got most of the referendum observers on these coaches. And Lieutenant Colonel Dimitrijevic in his car, followed by my car, we set off to try and get these observers out of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just conclude with tab 6 on the second page. You report, halfway down the page: The results of the meeting of the Presidency eased the situation as a lot of the SDS demands were met by the government, and you set out what was met.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you refer to a meeting of the Presidency, does that mean that the Presidency including members of all parties?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No. At that stage, I was looking upon Ejub Ganic basically as the representative of the Presidency that I was dealing with, because it was getting less frequent for the various ethnic groups to actually talk together. So if we had a meeting with the Serbs, they were separate. When we arrived first in the mission area we were able to talk to all of these people together, but it was becoming increasingly difficult with the amount of mistrust so we found ourselves dealing with them separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you got the election monitors out. I think the journey took several hours to make, although it was only a couple of miles, or three miles or something like that, but on the following day, the 3rd of March - paragraph 21 - what happened within the city by way of Muslim-erected barricades?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was informed on the 3rd of March that a lot of barricades were now going up in certain portions of the city. Not the entire city but those parts of the city that were predominantly occupied by Muslims. I didn't see any of them myself, but when I inquired I was informed that there was a great fear that Serb paramilitaries under the command of Arkan were coming towards Sarajevo. I understand it was from Pale, I was informed. I have no evidence of this. And I had heard of Arkan's reputation and I attempted to ascertain if in fact this report was true. The only information I received subsequent to that in relation to Arkan was that a member of the hotel staff informed me that Mr. Arkan was anxious to meet with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you ever able to verify whether Arkan had made such a request?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I was not able to verify it at all and I was not able to verify if in fact Arkan had been in the city. All I know is that his reputation was such that it certainly spread a lot of concern among some of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 24. The Muslim barricades came down when and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The I think the Muslim barricades came down on the following day, on the 4th of March. I think the reason for this was there was a debate on television, Mr. Ganic, General Kukanjac, who was the senior JNA military officer in Sarajevo, and I think that took some of the tension out of it. And an address that had been made by Vice-president Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a delegation -- or the Cutileiro delegation on March the 15th and 16th for another round of talks on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You were available to but did not attend those talks; correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this in line with your retention of some independence so that you could carry out your task and be trusted by as many as possible?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I felt this was important, and I had no official capacity as -- at that stage as a member of the peace conference. I was strictly head of the monitor mission and reported through my chain of command to Zagreb. But I felt that it would be incumbent upon me to assist in any way I could with the visits and also in my dealings with the force commander of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was happening to movements around Sarajevo, in and around Sarajevo at this time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Movement was gradually becoming more difficult. A lot of the JNA movement had been brought about by the withdrawal of the JNA army, in essence, from Croatia. Part of the monitor mission's task at that stage was to follow the convoys of JNA as they came out of Croatia and ascertain where they were going to. As head of the mission, I was becoming concerned that as the JNA left Croatia, there was a large build-up of JNA forces into Bosnia, and it was around that time that I became aware of the -- I suppose the evidence that a lot of the JNA army who were from Bosnia originally would now become part of a JNA Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course not so very long before you had heard complaint of armaments in the form of rockets coming up from Montenegro also onto Bosnian territory.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was also concerned that with the result of the referendum and some of the comments that had been passed to me in relation to Dr. Karadzic and what would happen, I was anxious that we in the mission would receive information very quickly, if recognition was going to be given to Bosnia, so that I could develop a plan of evacuation for the people I had responsibility for. So I was very -- I was very conscious of wishing to be informed as to what the developments were and of following developments closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this tour of duty with the ECMM ended on the 22nd of March; Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Lord Carrington, whom you'd met in the course of this duty, asked you to become his personal representative, and in that capacity you returned as soon as the 10th of April, 1992, with Ambassador Cutileiro; correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you then had the opportunity, or indeed the duty, of meeting the senior politicians on a more regular basis even.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your return in April, what did you notice about the position in Sarajevo generally as compared with how it had been when you left at the end of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I found a dramatic difference in the whole atmosphere when I returned on the 10th of April. The first thing we noticed was that Sarajevo airport was under the complete control of the federal army. And the second thing I noticed was that there was a large crowd of inhabitants of Sarajevo eagerly seeking to leave the city. We soon established that -- that afternoon, that the only flights that were leaving Sarajevo were basically moving out members of the JNA and their families and that it was very difficult to get a flight for a civilian who wished to leave the city. There was an air of tension around, and it was very palpable, I felt. It was completely different to the atmosphere when I left as head of the monitor mission on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any sniping?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when the sniping started, but I do -- I was aware that UNPROFOR were finding it difficult and that positions had been entrenched. But I can't accurately reflect as to when the first incidence of sniping happened in the city to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At some stage certainly the term "Sniper Alley" came to be used, did it not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that was a frequent phrase which brought a lot of fear to a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may or may not be a phrase of precise definition. What, if anything, did you understand by it? You may have not been in the best geographical position to know it too well, but what did you understand it to mean?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I never actually moved into the city too much. I was very conscious of the instructions that were given to me by Lord Carrington which was that it was important that I remain safe and that I was a representative of the peace conference, but certainly I used to hear many reports from military people, from civilians, and certainly from members of the media that it was a dangerous place to drive along Sniper Alley, which I took to be a portion of the main road coming in towards the Marsal Tito barracks, around the Holiday Inn and up towards the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pretty well in the dead centre of the map --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- on the board, on that long road. Very well. I think one of the journalists you spoke to was Martin Bell. Do you remember an exchange with him on the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Can I just have that again? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Martin Bell.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember discussing matters with him on the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I know that when I arrived, we were going into immediate talks with the Serb leadership in the hotel in Ilidza, and I was quickly taken aside by Martin Bell, whom I had not met before, and he said to me, "Please remember that I have evidence of 25.000 refugees on the move from Zvornik." I asked him where did he get this information, and he said that he filmed it on BBC's television, their own camera which was out there. And I bore that in mind, and sometime during our discussions with Radovan Karadzic, I put it to him that I had received a report from there were 25.000 refugees on the move in Zvornik. He seemed to be a little bit alarmed when I gave him this information. He asked me where I got the information from. I told him it was given to me by BBC television, and he replied that he didn't trust them and didn't believe them. I mentioned later on to Martin Bell that I had in fact mentioned this to the Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you based for this mission; the same hotel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I stayed in the same hotel because I felt it would be of benefit. I would have had the facilities of the mission transport and communications, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you notice at some stage a change in the ethnic composition of the hotel staff?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. While I was in the capacity as Carrington's representative and around that time, I can't be sure exactly when, we noticed that a lot of the hotel staff had changed, and when I inquired about it, I was told that all non-Serbs who were members of the staff were dropped in a transport into the centre of Sarajevo. I asked a member of the hotel staff why this was the case and he said, "Well, we were told it was for their own safety." The following day, I think, I was invited to a dinner in the hotel by what I was told was the new Serb local community committee, and some members of the monitor mission were invited as well. I attended the dinner, but when I listened to a speech by this new chairman, whose name I do not know, I felt that we were being used to more or less accept this situation. So when I had an opportunity to respond to the speech, I stood up and I spoke about my concern at this development, and then I walked out from the dinner and invited the monitor mission personnel to follow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there was, on the 12th of April, a meeting organised by General Morillon which came to nothing because the SDS didn't turn up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were at that meeting. You went back to the Hotel Bosna and had discussions with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was that all about? We can see the fruits of it at tab 16 in the Exhibit 515.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, this was a period when we were attempting to negotiate cease-fires because firing had been quite frequent at this stage. And I was involved in negotiating a cease-fire agreement which is as is indicated on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says here the leaders of the three main parties, aware of the extremely serious situation, agree. Had you been dealing with them individually or collectively?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: We had been dealing with them individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It has the terms of the cease-fire, which includes, we see towards the bottom of the page, disbanding all irregular armed forces in accordance with an agreed timetable under the supervision of the EC monitors. And in this context it concludes the three main parties reaffirm their opposition to any territorial gain by force and agree on the right of return to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I should point out that this agreement was officially negotiated not by myself but certainly by the visiting delegation of Jose Cutileiro and his officials. But I was a member of the delegation at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 33 of the summary. Did you conduct negotiations with the board of Sarajevo Television about a clause of this agreement allowing access to the television station? You may not find it here.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was to -- part of the agreement was that this would be done, so on the following day, on the 13th of April, I went to Sarajevo Television, and I had some Serbs can me. I can't recall who they were, but they were -- they were to be there on behalf of what we were considering during the cease-fire. So I chaired this meeting, and I soon realised that what I interpreted to be the terms of the cease-fire as related to television wasn't what the Serbs had actually wanted. We understood that the terms of the cease-fire included that the Serbs would be given more access to television air time, but in fact it became clear during the meeting that what the Serbs wanted was a division of all of the assets of Sarajevo Television. This would include parts of the buildings, parts of the facilities. And nothing came of this because it was my understanding this was not what had been agreed during the cease-fire. So the meeting did not achieve anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same general topic, on the 18th of April, did the Sarajevo Television receive a telephone call making a certain threat?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that briefly.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was informed by a phone call I received from Sarajevo Television that they had received a warning from Pale, the Serbs in Pale, that if they did not get off the air, the television station would be targeted in 30 minutes. Now, at that time, the Bosnian Serb Crisis Committee of Dr. Radovan Karadzic had based themselves in the hotel where I was, so I attempted to contact Dr. Karadzic, who was downstairs, and I got in contact with one of his aides and I told him that I wanted Dr. Karadzic to ensure that this attack would not take place on the television station, and the aide came back and told me that Dr. Karadzic wished to assure me that this attack would not take place. Approximately 20 minutes later, the television station was hit by mortar fire, and I understand two people were killed. I sent a message to Dr. Karadzic that I was now going to condemn this attack and blame him or that he would take responsibility for it because it was he who assured me that this attack would not take place. So I sent the message to him, and later on that evening he came to me with Nikola Koljevic, in a very agitated state, and he said to me that -- he admitted that the attack had taken place, he admitted to me that it was done by Serbs or Serb paramilitaries, but that it was not done with his permission, and that he said he would carry out an investigation. But I got the impression he was very embarrassed by what had happened and was very concerned when I told him that I would condemn this attack on BBC television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Something I think you did.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But did he, despite his confess-and-avoid approach to this, did he say where the attack had been ordered from?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you discover where it had been ordered from?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not discover nor did I seek to. I was -- I assumed that because Radovan Karadzic admitted it had taken place, that it would have been from -- directed by Pale from some position forward of that that would have been within mortar fire, or that the television would have been within mortar fire. Of course, this is not the first time this happened. It happened subsequently on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, do you think or do you believe now that there was a way for Mr. Karadzic to prevent such an attack at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour, it would have been my -- it would have been my acceptance at the time that he was the undisputed leader of the Serbs. He had been many occasions in Pale. He operated a lot from Pale. So I would have been satisfied that he had a lot of influence as to what did and did not take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be those ways for him to prevent, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would direct his military commander to ensure it didn't happen, or he would direct the paramilitaries in Pale to ensure it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you mean that he had direct influence over paramilitaries in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that His Honour would want to know on what other experience or what other material you formed the view that Karadzic had the ability to control the military or the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, it was around this time when the -- when we would have talks in the Hotel Bosna with the Serbs that they would come under the protection of armoured cars provided by the JNA. And on one occasion we had a meeting with Radovan Karadzic and General Aksentijevic and both of them travelled together in an armoured car, so it would have been my assumption that he had a lot of control and influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it may be, just to focus on this topic in a wider, general setting, did you have any evidence one way or another, or material pointing one way or another to the suggestion that the armed forces, regular or paramilitary, were acting without political oversight?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would have to say that in my opinion at that time, the JNA, although a large influence and present, were not directly getting involved in any conflict. But certainly they were everywhere. There was a gradual build-up, and that increased as the evacuation from Croatia progressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 37. Beg your pardon, paragraph 36. Can you deal with something specifically although it may have a wider, general application: Was there an occasion when an ECMM team was sent to Foca having received, or some part of the mission having received reports of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the ECMM mission headquarters office when a decision was made to attempt to send a team to Foca because information was coming in, "ethnic cleansing" was a phrase that becoming more frequent, and I assumed that the monitor mission received some reports of events that were taking place in Foca. I did not have any influence in this except that I was aware that it was happening, and within the short period of time after the team departed for Foca, they returned. I spoke with one of them who was an Italian officer and he informed me that they were stopped by the JNA and told that the JNA could not ensure their safety or their security if they went to the Foca region, and therefore, they were taking the decision not to allow them to proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you raise this matter with Nikola Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Nikola Koljevic was quite sympathetic and a man who used to ramble quite considerably I found, but he did say that he would like to be able to facilitate the monitor mission because he believed in what they did, and he said he would even offer to go to Foca himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, was this -- I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: But he didn't go, of course, nor did the mission go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did this explanation or excuse or reason for non-access to areas, or to this area, where ethnic cleansing was under consideration on grounds of security, was that something that happened once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was beginning to happen increasingly. Certainly I had a report from the area of Banja Luka by one of my teams that they were now finding freedom of movement very difficult. Now, the two binding principles under which the monitor mission were in Bosnia, apart from their specific tasks, was that the authorities in Bosnia would provide freedom of movement and safety and security. This was an unarmed mission totally, therefore they didn't pose a threat to anybody. And in order to be able to keep up-to-date on the developments politically and militarily, they needed to get to areas. And certainly I was aware that the monitor mission was becoming increasingly frustrated by the lack of progress in their teams going to certain areas. Also around this time we became aware that everything -- there was a lot of reference to ethnic cleansing and there were refugees on the move, and it was becoming very difficult for the mission to move anywhere; and this would have been one of those occasions, when they attempted to go to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 21st of April was there fierce fighting in the area outside the Hotel Bosna where you were located, and as you could judge it was it Bosnians firing into an adjoining location with Serbs returning fire?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. The area where I lived was the Hotel Bosna in Ilidza and it was predominantly a Serb area. The first occasion that I witnessed any fighting in the city happened outside our hotel at about 5.00 a.m. in the morning of April -- in fact, my record I think has it on April the 22nd. And I, after a while --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can take it quite shortly just because I have got an eye on the clock.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I know that fighting took place. We could see Serb paramilitary returning fire, but we could also see a lot of fire coming in against the Serb paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 13 people died in that battle, I think.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: We were told that 13 people died, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 38. On the 23rd of April, did Lord Carrington with Ambassador Cutileiro and president of the Council of Ministers of the European Union, Dr. Pinhiero, arrive at Sarajevo airport for talks of a cease-fire and was the text of the 12th of April cease-fire reaffirmed?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there meetings between that delegation and UNPROFOR Generals MacKenzie and Morillon and the JNA Commander Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Together with representatives Mr. Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and Koljevic and Boras for the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you left with the task of getting that ceasefire agreement signed and on terms that everybody did it at the airport?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Karadzic signed first because he was at the airport --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously the interpreter cannot follow. The interpreter is only reading the transcript with a delay. Because both the witness and Mr. Nice speak the same language, you should warn them to make small pauses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for the suggestion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Karadzic the first to sign and did Izetbegovic initially decline to return to the airport but you persuaded him?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a pause in the fighting when the negotiators were in the city that day?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. There was no shooting going on that day until after the delegation left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At 9.00 p.m., what happened?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: At 9.00 p.m. a lot of gunfire broke out, and we persisted with attempting to get the party leaders back to sign the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, you received a phone call from a Mrs. Banjac, pleading that she should make some effort -- or that you should make some effort to release her husband, Jasenko Banjac, who had been abducted by the Serb police, she understanding that he had been taken for interrogation in Serb-held Vraca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to do anything about that? Was this something that Pale was able to deal with and control?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was in Pale sometime later, and I raised this issue and I was told that it was likely that this man would be released, thereby giving me the impression that they were aware that he was in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'd been identified as somebody to chair meetings at a local level between all three parties on a daily basis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct. This came from a peace conference which we had in London on one of the sessions, and the peace conference was anxious to find out if there was any level at which representatives from the three sides would sit down together. So I would was proposed as a chairman, and that was accepted by the leadership of three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see the composition of this regular meeting at tab 9, which was annex 8 but is tab 9 of the exhibit. It sets out the composition there, but in fact I don't think it met very often, this particular commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. It was difficult to get them all together because of the continuous fighting in the city, but we had met on just a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move on, and I'm going to try and pick up the pace a bit if I can. On the 28th of April, you were involved in getting President Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Izetbegovic to Lisbon for the peace negotiations. You managed to get him, with difficulty, to the airport, and then you were told something about airspace or the use of airspace.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: When we took the president under United Nations escort as far as the airport, I was anxious to get him there before dark. When we arrived at the airport, the aircraft that was to take him to Lisbon had not landed. I inquired from the manager of the airport and he told me that because Belgrade controlled the airspace over Bosnia, they had to get permission from Belgrade for the aircraft to land and Belgrade refused permission. So we had no alternative but to take the president back into the city under UN escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, he got out of the following morning?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, we managed to get him out the following morning at approximately 1000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 10 is the next exhibit we'll look at. While we're turning that up, I think on the 28th of April, you met the mayor of Sarajevo, Mr. Kresevljakovic to discuss access to food stores in the city's suburbs.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The letter that we can now see follows on from that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. A copy of that letter was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Explain its setting, please, for us.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding is that the letter was addressed to Mr. Jack Delor, who was the president of the European Union, and notated on the top of the letter in handwriting was copies to Mr. Cutileiro, Mr. Soares, who was a member of the peace conference, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now again we can look at the letter in detail ourselves. We can see at the foot of the first page the mayor's account of kidnapping innocent inhabitants, civilians and children, threats of blackmail, they exchanged them for snipers and other attackers, captivated, it says, by territorial defence, and indeed over the page you see six lines up from the bottom his description as mayor of the exhausted city. This letter, which as I say we can all read at leisure, accurate or overstating or what?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It would be my opinion that the letter was probably overstated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But with an underlying factual base?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 45. On the 30th of April, did you have a meeting with Bosnian acting Prime Minister Mr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I met with Mr. Mahmutcehajic in his office. He was the acting Prime Minister on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he gave you something then?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, he gave me a transcript of a phone conversation which he said was between Dr. Nikola Koljevic, who was in Lisbon for the peace talks, and a Mr. Karisik who was believed to be in the area of Pale. I'm not familiar with this gentleman, so I don't know. And the transcript centred around a requirement for the people in Pale to show me evidence of the moving back of artillery positions which were overlooking the city because this was negotiated in Lisbon as part of the continuing process, and Dr. Koljevic intimated that if I as Carrington's representative did not see evidence of the withdrawal of this artillery, then the peace talks in Lisbon would be suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you were provided simply with a written transcript at that time and you were, I think, unable to verify one way or another whether the written transcript reflected any real conversation or not.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yesterday you'd been able to hear an intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to identify any of the voices?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I identified the voice of Dr. Nikola Koljevic only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And therefore, the transcript which you provided, which we can find as one of your original annexures, annex 10 at tab 11, is something you're now better able to verify as apparently being accurate?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at tab 11, and you may want your pointer for the map. I know this was not the map you were looking at overnight when you were reviewing this transcript. Are you going to be able to identify approximately, for the advantage of the Judges, the two positions that we've been able to pick out?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Here is one here, Zlatiste, and the second one is Vraca, which is very close into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first place, how many kilometres from the city would that be?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would say this is not more than a kilometre and a half, maximum, from the city. The other one, Vraca, is right on the outskirts of the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just look how those places turn up in the transcript itself. "N" is Nikola Koljevic and "M" is Mladjo Karisik. The first reference to Milenko presumably referring to Karisik one way or another. And he says: "We can't get through to Pale. What did they do? What kind of an action happened yesterday? The conference stopped because of that shooting. I see there's nothing from Zlatiste." And that's the first place you've been referring to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through all of it because we can see another reference to an artillery position or firing position in the middle of the page: "From Hum, from Zlatiste, from Sirokaca direction." You haven't been able to locate that, I think.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if we go further down the page, we see reference to yourself with Koljevic speaking: "Listen, you should take care of that today. We agreed with Doyle to get the observers on the place where our artillery stands. Let that artillery withdraw. We can't start the conference here without doing that. That they are casing it to us here and it should be like that in order that we can attack him. They do not have the argument, these here are talking only about the artillery..., then demobilisation can be allowed. We must drive him into a corner here. Doyle will appeal to you and you will take him to some artillery points." The reply: "Theirs?" "No, not theirs, ours, it is written like that on the paper, demobilisation cannot start until the artillery that threatens the town is taken away. They permanently state it that it can shoot at the city. And not one shell could fall on the city any more. We can't prove that it comes from Hum, we can only take them there and tell them: These are our artillery weapons. I ask you to do that and to accompany them and let them come to some of our artillery points." "Ours?" "Ours."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm slowing down. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "You know that our artillery is situated on Vraca." And I think Vraca was the second place you indicated, closer to the city.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed it can be seen on the black and white map. Very well. That's all I ask of that. I'm sorry to have gone too fast. On that same day, I think, the 30th of April, did you go to Pale to meet Mrs. Plavsic, to observe artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I had attempted to go to Pale the day before, which was the 30th of April, but we weren't able to make progress up on the route to Pale because the route was totally congested with tanks that were heading up to Pale. So Mrs. Plavsic agreed with me that we would come back down and we would attempt to go up on the following day, which we did on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you had a conversation with her, she picking you up -- or you picking her up outside her apartment block?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what did she say about territory and percentages and things like that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: In the course of conversation with her, she intimated to me that it was important that if there was to be a division of territory in Bosnia, it should accurately reflect the ethnic groupings. She also mentioned that the Serbs should be entitled to about 70 per cent or 75 per cent of the territory because even though they had a smaller percentage ethnic-wise, the fact that they had lost a lot of territory since the war and the fact that they were mainly rural people would indicate that they deserved more territory than the other groups. She also casually mentioned to me that if it took the lives of 3 million people to solve this problem, then maybe they should get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so her justification for the larger percentage of territory was that the others were city dwellers or city-centred dwellers?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Specifically, did she identify the ethnic group that was that minority of city dwellers?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: She did make reference to the Muslims as being mainly city dwellers and business people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think at some stage you sent your colleague out to attempt to check on artillery positions. It was your birthday then or thereabouts, and you calculate that something of a public relations exercise was made out of that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I indicated to Mrs. Plavsic that when I was going to Pale, I needed to be careful that my visit to Pale was not to be exploited as to be taken as some sort of recognition of the -- what became Republika Srpska. So I told her that I would go to Pale to meet some of the leadership but I did not want any publicity.
