She was aware of the fact that it happened to be my birthday, so when I sent my deputy out to verify the withdrawal of the artillery positions, we had a discussion with some of the leadership in the location, at the end of which, after dinner, a birthday cake was rolled into the room and a video camera suddenly appeared to videotape the event, and I felt that I had been exploited to the extent that I understand that this appeared on Belgrade television the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You met up with your deputy who had been attempting to verify withdrawal of artillery positions. He didn't speak to you in the presence of Bosnian Serb officials but reported to you in the car on the way back what?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: He informed me that he had no evidence of the withdrawal of any artillery, and on receipt of that information I contacted Lisbon and gave them that report, and I understand it resulted in the subsequent disbandment of the talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that's a convenient moment, we'll adjourn. Colonel Doyle, in this and any other adjournment, I must warn you as we warn all witnesses, please don't speak about your evidence to anybody and that does include the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move to paragraph 50, something not on the summary, relates to the 2nd of May. I think on the 2nd of May, Colonel, Izetbegovic returned as a result of something that was said to you, you weren't expecting him. He was arrested in circumstances fairly well known and was subsequently released?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was it that was said to you that led to his being unattended by you at the airport?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: When I was taking the president to the airport, it was done with a security escort from the United Nations, and the arrangement was that when the president returned, the Presidency would inform me and I would arrange for the United Nations escort to return to the airport to take him back. On that day in question, and there was a lot of fighting that started in the city, and I got this phone call from what I thought was the Presidency saying that because of the renewed fighting in the city the president would not be coming back on that occasion. So I phoned the United Nations and told them to stand down the escort. I later realised that the phone call I received was not from the Presidency but was from other source who wanted me to ensure that the escort did not arrive at the airport and I found out subsequently that the president did return to Sarajevo and was taken into custody by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Along with his daughter and things like that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Along with his daughter and another member of the Presidency whose name I can't recall and his security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the released was conditioned on withdrawal from barracks, I think?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. And it became something of a -- the negotiations for his release centred around he being released and also taking the cordon that was around the military headquarters where General Kukanjac was now a hostage in his own headquarters, that was the deal, that one would be released and the cordon around the headquarters would be lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 50. On the 5th of May you participated in cease-fire negotiations involving Fikret Abdic, Stjepan Kljuic, and General Aksentijevic on the Serb side. Any inclusion of the Bosnian Serbs? If not, why not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs did not come to those negotiations primarily because they didn't deem it safe to be able to go to that portion of the city which was the PTT building which was the headquarters of the UNPROFOR, and therefore we continued the negotiations between the members that you mentioned and Mr. Fikret Abdic, Stjepan Kljuic, and the JNA under General Aksentijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 17 shows the fruits of this negotiation, limited though they were, because I think the cease-fire was really the same day, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to say that a lot of these cease-fires were broken fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, tab 17 --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: But we did -- I did get an agreement from the various parties, and it was signed as you see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 10th of May -- I should have asked you this: Your impression at this stage as to the desire of the JNA was that it wanted to do what?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was -- I was satisfied at this stage that the JNA wished to withdraw from Bosnia in totality, and my view was I think reinforced when I went to Belgrade subsequently and spoke with two senior officers of the JNA who wished to talk to me. So that -- they were my impressions, that the JNA wished to withdraw from Bosnia, in a dignified manner I would add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I move to the 10th of May. I think there was another tentative agreement reached on the evacuation of the JNA barracks in the city. This has been dealt with an earlier exhibit, Exhibit 503, tab 18 for which courtesy copies are available and a copy for the witness. This agreement concerned leaving weapons and heavy equipment behind; correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who wanted that equipment to be left behind?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My impression would have been that if these heavy weapons were left behind, it will be taken over the non-Serbs, because at that stage I recall a conversation with the vice-president saying that he was very anxious to try and get weapons for the defence of the city, for the Muslims. So I assume that one of the advantages of the JNA leaving all their heavy weapons would be that it would be taken over by some other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That then the 10th of May we needn't spend any longer on that document which has been reviewed before. On the 12th of May were you evacuated by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The decision had been made to withdraw the monitor mission from Bosnia, and early that morning I was informed that -- in fact the night before I was informed by the -- my successor as head of the monitor mission for Bosnia that I was to be taken out of the city. I do not know who arranged that I would fly, that the JNA would fly me to Belgrade. But I was advised that I should be at the PTT building at 0530 hours the following morning. That was the morning of May the 12th. I was taken to the military barracks at Lukavica, and the JNA flew me from Lukavica to Belgrade. I was in the company of General Aksentijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the way, your path took you where?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: When we were taking off from Lukavica, I was informed by General Aksentijevic that the helicopter would be touching down in Pale first because there was a requirement to take a soldier who was dying from wounds back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will know where Pale is and can find it on page 33 of the atlas if it wishes to, due east of -- in fact due east of Sarajevo, Exhibit 336. On your way to Pale, what did you notice by way of artillery?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, on the way to Pale I was conscious of seeing a very large amount of artillery weapons, mortars, and they were deployed along the mountain ridge outside of Sarajevo, because the aircraft was flying relatively low. I didn't pass any comment to General Aksentijevic on seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your interpretation of the fact that the aircraft was confident enough to fly low over this artillery -- these artillery positions being what?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I assumed they were artillery -- Serb artillery positions, because if they weren't, the helicopter would not have been flying as low as it was. Had they been -- had they been belonging to the Muslims or Croats, I'm sure they would have attempted to shoot down the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move to Belgrade. Before we do, you didn't, I think, in Belgrade meet any of the Bosnian Serb leaders, did you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On review of your own working documents of the time, are you able to help us with whether those Bosnian Serb leaders had Belgrade locations where they could be found?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I know that I have in my diary telephone numbers for all of the party leaders, and in reviewing my diary recently, I noticed that when I was given the telephone numbers of Radovan Karadzic and Nikola Koljevic, I was also given Belgrade telephone numbers for them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On arrival in Belgrade, was your early appointment or one of your first appointments with Vladislav Jovanovic, with whom you had dinner?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th of May, when I was withdrawn from Bosnia, somebody had arranged that I would have dinner with Foreign Minister Jovanovic. I assume this came from Mr. Jovanovic's office himself, and I had dinner with him that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he make a comment about Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- he was very gracious in his comments to me, but in the course of the conversation that evening, he said that -- he asked me how I found, in general, the Bosnian Serbs. So I gave him my opinion, and then he replied by saying, "Well, you know, there are far more radical Serbs than the people you have been dealing with." So when I asked him what was he referring to, he just made a reference to the people in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 56 we've covered. Paragraph 57. On the 20th of May did you fly to Lisbon, having been invited to join the peace talks, and did you stay there until they failed on the 27th of May, but within the course of that time and as a result of an event that happened in Sarajevo, did you achieve something about Sarajevo airport? Tab 18 refers.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: We were in Lisbon for some days, and we didn't seem to be making any progress on talks with the representatives of the parties. And then on the 27th of May, a mortar landed in a bread queue in Sarajevo, causing several fatalities. This became an item of immediate news. Cutileiro's delegation, which included myself, were contacted and told to turn on television, and we saw the results of this mortar explosion. A short time after that, Radovan Karadzic was very anxious to come in and talk with us, and we had a discussion about meeting with him. So when he came in, he immediately inferred that the Bosnian Serbs were not responsible for that mortar. I recall Ambassador Cutileiro saying to him -- asking him how was he -- how did he know that this attack could not be attributed to the Bosnian Serbs, because it was impossible to have contact with Sarajevo from Lisbon. However, what was attempted by the conference as a result of this was that Dr. Karadzic was informed that whether the Serbs were to blame or not, they -- the Serbs were actually responsible for it or not, they were probably going to be blamed and, therefore, it would be the interest of them to make a gesture to our conference. We had discussed this previously to Dr. Karadzic coming in, and I suggested - I think it was I, I may not be sure on that - but one of us suggested that maybe we would exploit this to be able to get an agreement on the airport. So after some considerable time, Dr. Karadzic agreed that in certain circumstances he would be willing to hand over control of Sarajevo airport to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see on tab 18 the leadership announcing its readiness to open the airport for humanitarian transports and other details of that. It's also announcing its readiness to remove heavy artillery from around Sarajevo under international supervision. Similar supervision will be extended to the city to ensure the protection of the civilian population. Very well. Paragraph 59. You returned on the 2nd of June to Belgrade, and you met Lieutenant Colonel Dimitrijevic, he in civilian clothes. You had another meeting with Jovanovic. You believe that was set up by Dimitrijevic. And on leaving Jovanovic, you saw somebody in his outer office. Now, what position did Jovanovic hold at this stage?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was concerned, Jovanovic was Foreign Minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who did you see?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: When I left his office and in the outer office waiting to go in, or I assumed he was waiting to go in, was a newly appointed minister of the -- what became the Republika Srpska, a Mr. Buha, whom I had previously met in Pale. So I knew him to be a minister of the Bosnian Serb Republika. And I noticed him sitting in the outer office, and we just acknowledged each other but we did not speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. On the 12th of June did the same Lieutenant Colonel Dimitrijevic indicate that the accused was prepared to or wanted to meet you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. He came to me and said that -- that Slobodan Milosevic would like to meet with me, and I assumed it would be at some meeting with many, many people. But when he told me that Mr. Milosevic would meet me at a time that suited me, I then began to realise that maybe this was to be a private meeting. So I eventually did meet with Mr. Milosevic on the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You took along William Jackson from the British embassy as a note taker?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 12 contains your report. It's probably better if I read most of this out, I think, and I'll try and go at the correct speed. You set out how you spoke to the accused according to instructions. In a lengthy monologue the accused argued in familiar terms that the Serbs were being unjustly blamed for everything happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina, claiming that Belgrade shared the objectives of reopening Sarajevo airport, internationalising the city, and neutralising the artillery in the mountains. Belgrade had repeatedly made this clear Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. through public statements. He also strongly recommended Karadzic's idea that UN monitors should be attached to Bosnian Serb units to verify the situation on the ground. There was no regular or irregular forces from Serbia itself on Bosnian soil, he said. Belgrade could not halt humanitarian aid to Bosnian Serbs but would take any concrete steps proposed by Lord Carrington in order to bring peace to the area. He agreed is that the EC conference was the only forum for the resolution of the crisis. A settlement was in Belgrade's interest, though the Muslims did not apparently see it to be in theirs. You record, Colonel, that there was no political discussion of issues such as sanctions or recognition. The press weren't present, and there had been no publicity. Following that summary, you deal with matters in a little more detail, setting out the next page, paragraph 3: You called for Belgrade's support in maintaining the cease-fire, reopening the airport, facilitating UN observers to neutralise artillery and halting expulsions of non-Serbs from occupied settlements. Paragraph 4, you stressed Lord Carrington's concern for the accused to use his influence over Serb irregulars in Bosnia-Herzegovina and over Mladic to end the shelling of Sarajevo, emphasising the importance of getting international agencies back into the city as soon as possible and pointing out the international consensus that the EC peace conference was the forum in which future constitutional arrangements should be elaborated. Having listened to you attentively, the accused said he believed Lord Carrington was aware that Belgrade was doing its best to support the peace process. In all communications with the Bosnian Serbs, Belgrade had pressed them to avoid bloodshed. Sarajevo was the key problem position, and if the city could be pacified, solutions would usually be easier elsewhere in the Republic. Belgrade, he said, shared the objectives of reopening the airport, putting the city under UN control, and removing the artillery. This had been made clear publicly and on repeated occasions, he said. It was now the turn of the UN to take action accordingly, and he expressed keen interest in knowing when the airport might be reopened and indeed when Lord Carrington might visit Sarajevo. He endorsed the proposal from the Bosnian Serb leader Karadzic that observers be attached to each unit of the Bosnian Serb forces in order to witness the fact on the ground. He said that Belgrade was constantly cast in the role of aggressor although there wasn't a single Serb from Serbia fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If the contrary were true, it would be impossible to keep secret, he said. Serbian police were monitoring the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as reported by the Ministry of Interior, a week ago had already arrested some 1.300 people who had been in the area carrying weapons for which they had no licence. He claimed he personally pressed for the evacuation of the JNA cadets from Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo even at the cost of leaving behind heavy weapons to the annoyance of local Serbs. He pointed out more than once that Belgrade had condemned the shelling of -- vigorously condemned the shelling of Sarajevo which had been a futile and criminal exercise for which the perpetrators should be punished. They would be if they set foot in Serbia, he said. He contrasted the activities of the Croats who had regular troops in Western Herzegovina, a fact which a French emissary had recently confirmed to him. And he rejected your suggestion, Colonel, that it had been the Serbs who had principally benefited from the arms and ammunition abandoned by the JNA, claiming that all ethnic groups had ended by securing a share. He stated that Belgrade could not halt its supply of humanitarian aid to the Bosnian Serbs in the form of clothing, food, tents and money, but complained that there had been no coverage by the Western media of two Serbian relief convoys which had distributed food and medical goods impartially to the three ethnic communities in Sarajevo. He agreed there was no alternative to the peace conference for working out a solution. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was impossible for anyone to emerge as a winner from war in the republic. There were no innocent parties, he said; Bosnia-Herzegovina was a state of three equal peoples and Belgrade would respect any agreement based on a tripartite consensus. The international community had been ill advised to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina when it did, but Belgrade was doing politically everything it could to bring about peace. It was obviously in its interests to do so, whereas for the Muslims, Izetbegovic was refusing to negotiate and seemed inclined to continue the civil war. Belgrade would take any concrete steps required of it to promote a settlement. Thus the notes typed up, I think, by your colleague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One question on that: You expressed the view that the Serbs had obtained the largest share of weaponry. On what basis and did you hold it notwithstanding the accused's challenging of your position?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My feeling was that from my time as head of the monitor mission in Bosnia, President Izetbegovic had said that there would not be a requirement for people to obey the federal call-up to mobilisation. So the only people that were being called up in fact were Serbs. It had been brought to my attention in many of the opstina locations that I went to that the others - they being Croats and Muslims - were very concerned that these people who were being called up for mobilisation were being allowed to keep the weapons that were issued to them by the JNA army and that they were becoming very concerned by the fact that these people, the Serbs, were retaining their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We see a handwritten addition to the note. Your handwriting, I think.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When and how did that come to be put there?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: When Mr. Jackson came to me at my hotel the following morning with the written text of my meeting with Mr. Milosevic, I had recalled Mr. Milosevic acknowledging to me that Sarajevo was a Muslim city and that the Serbs bombarding it, that they should not do so because, basically, it was a Muslim city and the Muslims should have control over it. So I felt that was sufficiently important for me to put it in writing in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Coming to the conclusion of your evidence, then. Paragraph 62. You were in Brussels for a plenary session on the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia on the 13th of August, 1992, which lasted for two days, being aborted when the Bosnian Muslim delegation left; correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were in Brussels on the 16th of August still when the Times published a photograph -- Times newspaper published a photograph of a prisoner at barbed wire of the Omarska camp in an emaciated condition. You presented that to Karadzic while he was having breakfast at the same hotel.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Being approached thereafter by one of Karadzic's advisors, a Mr. Kennedy, seeking an appointment with you or meeting with you, you saying you couldn't meet him in an official capacity but nevertheless encountering Karadzic in the lobby of the hotel with Krajisnik, Koljevic, and the man Kennedy.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your impression?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My impression was that Radovan Karadzic was very taken back by the paper and the photograph which referred to the camps, and I felt that I should mention to him also that these camps would now become public notice. I mentioned to him that we were very familiar of the practice of forcing people to leave their homes, taking their homes over. These would be essentially non-Serbs. And some of these people were obliged to pay money for permission to leave their homes. Dr. Karadzic agreed with me that this was not legal and should not have happened. I suggested to him that maybe to set the record straight he might write a letter to the Times pointing out this fact. I got the impression that he said he would, and I am unaware if that in fact transpired because I returned to Belgrade the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You flew back to Zagreb on the 17th of August, to Sarajevo on the 20th of August, and on that day there was an artillery attack on the Marsal Tito barracks damaging vehicles including United Nations vehicles.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You met Mrs. Plavsic on the 22nd of August, and then you left Sarajevo on the 24th of August, travelling to Zagreb, making your way to London for the peace conference on the 26th and 27th of August, completing your duties in relation to these matters thereafter?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 19, please. If we can just lay that on the overhead projector. And a copy for the witness. While you've been here, Colonel Doyle, have you been able to assist us by listening to several tape-recordings of what are apparently intercepts of telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The purpose of that being to see if you're able to identify voices and in the way revealed on this table, you have been able to identify in most cases one voice, in one case two voices of people you were listening to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Court will see the references. The reference number on the left-hand side with a description of the telephone conversation, the apparent date of the conversation, and then the voice or voices identified by the witness, Karadzic, Koljevic, and on one occasion Karadzic and the accused. His evidence on that point and the intercepts to which he refers which follow on from tab 19 and are produced by him for these purposes and to this extent will be the subject of the overall intercept exercise at a later stage, but this is evidence of voice identification. It seems to us probably the most time efficient way to get witnesses to do the voice identification and produce the evidence in the form of a schedule and then consolidate all the material again at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment they'll only be marked for identification, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just looking at the exhibits, do we need in fact to exhibit them in this binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If there is no question as to continuity or identity, then they can probably -- everything after 19 could be removed from this binder because Exhibit 19 doesn't need to be for identification only because it's evidence of his identification. Sorry, tab 19. And the connection can be made with the exhibits themselves later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we'll do is we will leave them for the moment in the binder. So if there is any cross-examination upon them, it can take place and review the position at the end with that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll be asked further questions, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't understand this last point. Do you think that this witness can identify these intercepted conversations and prove their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He cannot prove the authenticity of the tape. All that he can do is to say that he's listened to the voices and he can identify them. If you want to ask him about that and cross-examine him about it, you can do so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Doyle, you came to Sarajevo on the 11th of October, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as a matter of fact, you were not only present there as a monitor which was your duty, you were quite familiar with things that were going on in Sarajevo, especially at this session of the Assembly in mid-October and after that, everything you testified about. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it correct that Serb members of parliament on that 15th of October put forth a request that this question of adopting a platform of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to exercise sovereignty, all these documents then the memorandum of sovereignty, the letter of intent and so on and so forth, that all of this should be presented before the council that dealt with issues related to the equality of rights of all the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina? This was a major issue, and they asked that before being debated in parliament this be discussed first before this council for the equality of rights of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was not aware at that time of the details of the political make-up within Sarajevo. I should point out that when I arrived there first I was just a monitor, and having been informed in Sarajevo that I would be deployed to Banja Luka, my -- I suppose my interest was in the area of Banja Luka during those early days. I was not involved at any national political level in those early days. So I would not be able to say the point that you raise, whether I was familiar with it or not, but I certainly at the time had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you had no knowledge of that and this was discussed at the Assembly session that you attended, is it correct that on that night, contrary to what was made public by Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly, that the session would be adjourned until the following morning when it was supposed to be continued, the vice-president of the Assembly, Mariofil Ljubic, said there would be a one-hour break and then Muslim and Croat MPs returned to the parliament hall and then in the absence of Serb MPs adopted this platform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't want to get mixed up here, but I should say that it was my recollection that that occurred during the parliamentary debate on whether or not there should be a referendum on independence, but that was not on -- my understanding was that was not on the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm talking about the key event involved. It doesn't really matter whether I have the exact date written down here. Do you remember that this parliamentary debate went on until 3.30 a.m. and that then Krajisnik, at 330 a.m., said that the session should be adjourned and continued the following morning at 10.00?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that Mr. Krajisnik said that it should be continued the following morning, but yes, I am aware that at that stage that the Serb delegation had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, the chairperson, that is to say the president of the parliament, said that the session would be adjourned and that it would be continued. It was already 3.30 in the morning and they worked all day, and he said the session would be continued the following morning at 10.00. And the others passed this decision in the absence of the Serb MPs. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was actually on the 24th of October. Is that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Again, I'm not too sure. I understand what you're saying, and I was there at the time, but I still don't think it was the 24th of October. But, yes, I do remember that occurring, and I do remember the parliamentary debate continued after the members of the Serbs had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Doyle. Can we clarify one point? The Serb representatives did not withdraw. When the president of the Assembly adjourned the session, then they left, and it was to be expected that the others would leave too because the session was supposed to continue the following day, the following morning. They did not leave the session. The president of the parliament said at 3.30 a.m. that the session would be adjourned, would be continue the following morning. Everybody got up and left. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was my understanding that certainly when the parliament was adjourned that the Serbs had left. You should remember that this whole debate was taking place in Serbo-Croat. I don't speak the language. I had an interpreter with me, and it was my understanding that the Croats and the Muslims decided on the adjournment of the Serbs that they would continue with the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 5, I have your report or, rather, what you sent, and at the end it says: "[In English] Note: It is expected that the legality of the Assembly being reconvened after it was closed by the Assembly president may be --" [Interpretation] not very legible -- "[In English] as may the authority of the president of the Assembly to conclude the session without a majority in the first place."

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I accept the accuracy of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That means that there is no doubt that the president of the Assembly closed the session. That is what is stated here in your report. So that fact is not being disputed.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then when the Serbs left in the belief that the session was adjourned and that it would be continued, then the Muslim and Croat MPs decided to continue the session without them and to pass a decision. Did you see that as something that could be treated as legal or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: A short period after that decision was made by the parliament, I sought a meeting with the judiciary of Bosnia to ascertain on the part of the Bosnian Serbs whether the parliamentary debate was constitutional or not, because the Serbs had mentioned to me that everything in the country was to be done by consensus. So I wanted to be able to give the monitor mission an accurate report on what the legality of this debate was. I had that meeting with the judiciary, and when I went to the meeting it was attended by the Deputy Minister for Defence. He asked me what was the purpose of the meeting and when I told him it was to ascertain whether the judiciary accepted that what went on in the parliament was constitutional, he told me that this was not what I should be seeking. When he left, I then put it to the members of the judiciary, and because one lady I spoke to who was a member said that we, the collective judiciary cannot decide whether that debate was constitutional or not because the judiciary are made up of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, so I could not get a definitive from the judiciary as to whether that decision was constitutional or not. And I did inform my headquarters of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you've just said yourself that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government consisted of representatives of all three peoples and that the rule was that decisions were passed by way of consensus between all three peoples. You were aware of that, and you just said so yourself. Is that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. What I said in relation to that was according Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the Serb leadership. It was the Serbs who told me that they were of the view that decisions had to be made by consensus of all three sides. So that was the Serb interpretation. And that was one of the reasons why I wanted to meet the judiciary, to ascertain whether or not that was constitutional. So the view that decisions had to be made by consensus of all three parties was referred to me by the Serb leadership, and not by the Muslims or the Croats. So in fact I don't know what was legal and what was not legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're not an expert in constitutional matters so I don't want to torment you any more with questions like that. Do you know that after that, precisely bearing in mind the fact that Muslim and Croat MPs, in violation of the constitution and rules of procedure, passed documents, enactments that were contrary to their interests or, rather, contrary to the interests of the Serb ethnic community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serb people, the Serb people being, in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one of the constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So bearing in mind the fact that the Assembly was abused to their detriment, on the 24th of October they founded their own Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I am aware that the Serb leadership, or that the Serb party founded their own Assembly. Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they then organised a plebiscite on the 9th and 10th of November, and a vast majority voted in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that before all these events and before the 14th and 15th of October and the 24th and 25th of January, 1992, Muslim and Croat representatives in the Assembly actually prevented the questions related to the equality of right of nations and nationalities from being on the agenda of this council that was supposed to deal with matters related to the equality of nations and nationalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was still in existence? If you don't know anything about this, just say so and we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in February 1991, the Party of Democratic Action made a draft declaration on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was submitted to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this caused quite a stir among many parties, especially in the Serb Democratic Party? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No. I wasn't -- I wasn't in Yugoslavia in February 1991. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the session of the 24th and 25th of January, 1992, the one you attended. Is it obvious that the presence of the Serb MPs, headed by the president of the Serb Democratic Party, Radovan Karadzic, at the session of the Assembly on the 24th and 25th of January, 1992, was an indicator of the will of the Serb side to ease tensions, to find a peaceful solution based on compromise which would satisfy the interests of all sides involved? So although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The witness can't answer long speeches. Colonel, can you help as to what's been put so far by the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that the Serbs had withdrawn from the day-to-day workings of the parliament in Bosnia, and I am aware that the Serb members of parliament did take place in that parliamentary debate, as referred to by Mr. Milosevic, on the 24th and the 25th of January, 1992, because I was present in parliament for that. The political manoeuverings around that time is not something that I would deem myself to be an expert on. Primarily as a military person, my function was to observe and to report, but the intricacies of government weren't something that I would be qualified to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it is beyond dispute that the Serb MPs, although this happened considerably after what you described when they left, they were nevertheless the present on the 24th and 25th of January, and they wanted to find a civil solution that would be acceptable to all. Is that the essence of what they were doing at that Assembly meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it quite clear that a concession was made on the Serb side in relation to their previous positions so that they would accept an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and the concession from the Muslim side to carry out a certain regionalisation? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would not term it as a concession. I would term it as a decision by the Serbs to take part in that parliamentary debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. According to what you said yourself, you were in close contact and you closely cooperated with Ambassador Cutileiro who, on behalf of the European Community, mediated in the negotiations between the representatives of the three sides, the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not take part in any of those debates at that stage because I was head of the monitor mission. It wasn't until I became Lord Carrington's representative that I was involved in negotiations. So in January 1992 I wasn't involved in any sessions or negotiations with Ambassador Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Even though you did not take part in the negotiations I, heard you say this morning that you closely followed everything that was going on. You observed this, and you reported on it. That is to say that you were informed about what was going on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: In general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you know too what was known throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, namely that Cutileiro became famous due to the plan for resolving the Bosnia-Herzegovnian crisis and on the 18th of March, 1992, all three sides had accepted that plan, that is to say before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Again, I'm not aware of that. I do know that the information I received was that the negotiation -- the negotiation team were very close to an agreement. I don't know whether an agreement was reached or not at that time. Because I wasn't part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do not remember that all three sides accepted that agreement and then afterwards, on the 25th of March, Alija Izetbegovic withdrew the signature that he had already placed on that plan?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I am not personally aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know at least that this plan envisaged that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be independent but regionally defined in accordance with the interests of all three peoples? That is how all three sides signed the agreement. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the most important event that occurred, this acceptance and then afterwards the withdrawal of Izetbegovic's signature from that plan. Is it possible that you don't know anything about this, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that many negotiations were taking place under the conference of Yugoslavia. My role at the time was to advise the negotiation team. I had no immediate hand in any of these negotiations. I was generally aware that negotiations were taking place. I was generally aware that some sort of an agreement had been reached or had hoped to be reached in or around the 18th of March. I am not familiar with the specifics of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are not even aware of the fact that all three sides accepted it on the 18th of March?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Personally, I am not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that even a Muslim newspaper wrote in mid-1993 that the non-acceptance of the Cutileiro plan was one of the most disastrous failures of the Muslim policy? They then wrote that the non-acceptance of the Cutileiro plan at the beginning of the negotiations that was even accepted by the Serbs shows how shortsighted the Muslim policy is. This is what their own Muslim newspaper said, the newspaper called Slobodna Bosna?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No. I am not familiar with the newspaper, and I am not familiar with the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember at least the rather widely known statement made by Izetbegovic on the 27th of February, 1991, in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm quoting this from a British newspaper. "[In English] ... Bosnia-Herzegovina but would not sacrifice its sovereignty for peace." [Interpretation] Do you remember that? This caused a great deal of concern. And then letters were sent to the Presidency of the SFRY because Yugoslavia was still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must have a chance to answer these questions. Colonel, do you know anything about these articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I know nothing about them. As I said before, I was not in Bosnia in February 1991, and have no knowledge of any letters of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you should deal with areas which the witness can himself give evidence about. He knows nothing about these articles. You will have the opportunity in due course to put evidence in front of us and if you wish you can put these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Since the witness doesn't know anything about the Cutileiro plan, and this had to do with the most important things that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you at least remember -- I mean, by then you were already there. On the 24th of February, 1992, the Sarajevo daily Oslobodjenje, that was a government-controlled newspaper of the then government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it carried a statement made by Jose Cutileiro at the beginning of the negotiating process, and this was at the Lisbon conference on the 21st and 22nd of February, 1992, that the Serbs were seeking a confederal Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the Croats were seeking a federation and that the Muslims were seeking an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you remember that statement at least?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Cutileiro plan did not envisage a confederal state but, rather, a cantonalised state, much firmer than a confederacy? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You do not remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do not remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You do not even remember that they accepted the Cutileiro plan and that all three sides accepted the Cutileiro plan? You do not remember that either?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us then move on to some things that you'd have to remember. In paragraphs 6 and 7 on page 11 of this statement that I received, and you said and I'm quoting you: On the 12th of April, General Morillon organised a meeting with all parties. We went to this meeting at 8.00 in the morning. In the command of the UN, Cutileiro had meetings with the president, Mr. Brkic, who represented the HDZ. General Kukanjac came on behalf of the JNA, and the ambassador talked to him too. The SDS did not appear at the meeting as expected. Nothing was achieved at that meeting. From that meeting we returned to the Hotel Bosna and we continued talking about a cease-fire with Dr. Karadzic. An agreement was reached on the wording of the ceasefire agreement. This wording was used later during that month when the agreement was finally signed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that text that you managed to agree upon with Karadzic at the Bosna Hotel was ultimately adopted later when the agreement was finally signed. And then in paragraphs 4 and 5 on the next page you say: "On the 23rd of April, Lord Carrington and Ambassador Cutileiro accompanied by the president of the Council of Ministers of the EU, Dr. Pinhiero arrived at the Sarajevo airport for talks. The text for a cease-fire was reaffirmed from the 12th of April. They had meetings with General MacKenzie and Morillon from UNPROFOR and the JNA commander General Kukanjac. The SDA was represented by Mr. Izetbegovic, the SDS by Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic and the HDZ by Mr. Boras. When Lord Carrington left he gave me the task of having the agreement signed. I had Dr. Karadzic sign first. That's what you say; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he signed it immediately. And then you go on in the text: "The president initially --" When you say "president," you mean Izetbegovic; isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The president initially refused to return, saying that his life could be in danger from snipers but I eventually talked him into returning to the airport, and he signed the agreement at about 8.00 p.m. that evening. So, Mr. Doyle, I quoted your very own statement, and doesn't this show that as far as the cease-fire is concerned, you did not have problems with the Serb side? The problem was precisely Izetbegovic who was dragging his feet on the attainment of this cease-fire; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I can acknowledge that Radovan Karadzic had no problem in signing the cease-fire. All I can repeat is that I was informed by President Izetbegovic that he was worried about his safety in coming to the airport. When I assured him he would be given a UN escort, he then agreed to come. He eventually arrived, and he signed the cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. From what you stated, the Serbs were militarily superior, and from that aspect, since you're a soldier, I assume that they didn't have such a need for it but they did want peace and were the first to sign. Karadzic was the first one to sign the agreement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, Karadzic was the first to sign the agreement, but for the main reason that he was only the party political leader who was still at the airport. Because when we spoke with the various political leaders, the last party we spoke to was Dr. Karadzic's party. So he was still there. My mission from Lord Carrington was to try and get the Croats and Muslims back to the airport to sign as was agreed. But Karadzic was still there, so it was automatic that he would sign the document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's assume that he didn't sign it first because he was right there. He could assume that he signed it because he was in agreement with the accord, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 on page 13 of your statement, you say: "On the 7th of April -- on the 27th of April, I received a call from Ambassador Cutileiro asking me if I could persuade Mr. Izetbegovic, on behalf of the SDA, and Mr. Brkic on behalf of the HDZ to travel to Lisbon for talks for the peace conference. Mr. Izetbegovic agreed to go with the UN escort to the airport, and an aircraft was arranged for their transport. Mr. Izetbegovic flew out to Lisbon on the 29th of April, at 11.20 a.m. Mr. Brkic, who had agreed earlier to travel to Lisbon, later on changed his mind." Two paragraphs later, you say that the Serb representative, Mr. Nikola Koljevic, was in Lisbon. So based on what you state here, Mr. Cutileiro called you and asked you if you could convince Mr. Izetbegovic and Brkic to come there and Koljevic was already in Lisbon, can we conclude that it was difficult to persuade the Croat and the Muslim side to go to the Lisbon negotiations? Otherwise, why would there be any need to convince them?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would conclude that the Serb leadership were already there. I think the problem mainly in relation to the Presidency was the physical difficulty of getting to the airport and the physical difficulty of getting an aircraft to take them to Lisbon. But yes, the Serbs were there first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, in paragraphs 2 and 3 on page 15, you've talked about things relating to the Lisbon negotiations. This is why it was strange to me that you don't know what the outcome was of the Cutileiro plan, and this is something that is generally known. But let's not go back to that. I am quoting you: "On the 20th of May I flew to Lisbon where I was invited to join the peace talks. I stayed there until the talks were aborted on the 27th of May. The most significant achievement of these talks was that Dr. Karadzic signed the agreement, signalling his intention to hand over the Sarajevo airport to the United Nations. On the 27th of May, a mortar shell killed a large number of people queueing for bread in Sarajevo. When this was published, Hari Silajdzic, who was the chief of the Bosnian Muslim delegation, stated that they would no longer continue with the talks. Immediately Dr. Karadzic, who was the head of the Bosnian Serb delegation, came to the room where we were negotiating and insisted that the Bosnian Serbs were not responsible for the mortar attack. Ambassador Cutileiro replied, asking Dr. Karadzic how would he know that they were not responsible because he had been in Lisbon all of the time. It was because of this mortar attack that Ambassador Cutileiro was able to exploit the situation and obtain the intention to hand over the airport. A statement to this effect was signed by Dr. Karadzic and this document was faxed to the United Nations in New York." I am quoting what you said. So the objective was to reach a peaceful solution, which would imply the agreement of all three sides. Is that correct, Mr. Doyle? The objective of the meeting was a peaceful resolution to which all three sides would agree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The only thing that was achieved at the meeting was that Radovan Karadzic agreed to hand over the Sarajevo airport to the UN troops for which only the accord of the Serbian side was necessary. Is that true, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim representative left the negotiations. This was the second time that the peaceful mediation by Mr. Cutileiro failed because of the refusal of the Muslim side to participate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. What I would have to say here is that the negotiation team were confident that once this attack took place in Sarajevo that the three parties would not remain at the table. It is true that Hari Silajdzic intimated that because of this attack the Muslims could not see themselves staying further. The objective of the team at that stage was to try to get something from these talks and it was decided then that one of the priorities in Sarajevo was to try and get access to humanitarian assistance and the only way that could be done was if the airport was taken over by an independent body that was recognised by us. And that is one of the reasons why it was suggested that as a gesture of good faith Radovan Karadzic would give us an indication that under certain circumstances the airport would be handed over to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back. I will now show you, because this is an extract in English, it's an article from the Independent from the 22nd of August, 1992, and it states: "[In English] Muslims slaughter their own people. The Independent, 720 words. From Leonard Doyle in New York." [Interpretation] Just by chance he happens to share your last name. Then he states -- I will not read the whole thing but I will show it to you, but I just wanted to point out a few things and you will be able to read whole thing for yourself. "[In English] United Nations officials and senior Western military officers believe some of the worst recent killings in Sarajevo, including the massacre of at least 16 people in a bread queue, were carried out by the city's mainly Muslim defenders, not Serb besiegers, as a propaganda ploy to win world sympathy and military intervention." [Interpretation] The text is quite long. It goes on to speak about the choreography and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow you to go on reading out what this Mr. Doyle says about it. You can ask the witness, since he is a military officer, whether he knows of this article and whether he shares these views. I think they have been described elsewhere, but for the moment you can ask the witness that, but you're not going to read a whole document out unless it's relevant to the witness's evidence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Do you know anything about this Mr. Doyle, first of all, Colonel Doyle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you've heard what he's suggesting, that the Muslims -- that senior, I should say senior Western military officers, and that might, of course, include yourself, believe that some of the worst killings, including this massacre to which you've referred in the bread queue, was carried out by the Muslim defenders. Now, you've heard that allegation, and of course you should have the opportunity to deal with it. Is there anything which you usefully think you can say about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I can say about it is that I am aware that this incident took place. I have absolutely no knowledge as to who caused it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you ever suggested to any reporters that the Muslims were killing themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to call Mr. Doyle, Mr. Milosevic, you can, or the officers who were referred to, but this witness can take this allegation no further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read one more sentence from this, and perhaps Mr. Doyle knows something about that, because the text ends in the following way: "[In English] UN force commander General Satish Nambiar concluded, however, that Bosnian forces loyal to President Alija Izetbegovic may have detonated a bomb. We believe it was a command detonated explosion, probably in a can a UN official said. The impact which is there now is not necessarily similar or anywhere near as large as we come to expect with a mortar round landing on the paved surface."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he knows nothing about this. Do you know the General who is referred to, General Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know of General Nambiar. He was the force commander in UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, look at this report. Look at this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There is no point. He knows nothing about this. He's said he cannot help you. If you want to call General Nambiar, as I say, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I intend to do that, Mr. May. Please don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May I now ask you, since you spoke about this and you described the conversation, and I quoted what Karadzic said about the same topic that you referred to, besides the fact that it's a tragedy that took place with the killing of these people in the bread queue, and it's really a terrible tragedy, does it not seem to you that this event could be the reason that this event could serve as a pretext to abandon this solution? Does that seem plausible to you? How could somebody back down from a peaceful resolution regardless of the tragic nature of this event? Is this not something that would seem absurd to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot possibly comment on this. The suggestion is - is this right so that we follow it - that this was used as a pretext to abandon the Cutileiro plan? Is that the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only the Cutileiro plan but a solution for peace anyway, because the Cutileiro plan was rejected. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness about it. Have you heard any such suggestion or is that something you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of it. It has never been suggested to me, and my professional opinion would be it had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time for an adjournment now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, you said yourself that you don't know anything about the Cutileiro plan or the signing or the abandoning of it. Do you at least know that a compromise solution was reached between the Serb and the Muslim side - i.e., Karadzic and Cengic - on the 24th and the 25th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the period when these negotiations were proceeding conducted by Ambassador Cutileiro, you were a representative of Lord Carrington; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I did not become a representative of Lord Carrington until the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at that point you were still the head of the monitoring mission.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now, please, could you take a look at paragraph 3 on page 9. You're talking about the setting up of barricades, and this is something that you talked about, the examination-in-chief, on the 2nd of March, 1992, in Sarajevo. Before that, the results of the referendum were published, and you say regarding the setting up of the barricades on the 2nd of March, 1992, the previous day, there was a murder where a Serb member of a wedding party had been shot to death by a Muslim in the centre of the city. This was also one of the reasons for an increase in the tensions within the Serb community. That is what you say. I assume that you recall that during the attack on the wedding procession Nikola Gardovic was killed. He was the bridegroom's father, and an Orthodox priest was wounded, Radenko Mitrovic. He was the brother-in-law of Gardovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly who was killed. All I know is that there was one Serb killed at least at that wedding. Their names I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you know that the man who was killed, whose name you don't know, his name is Nikola Gardovic, he was killed at the door of the Orthodox church in the centre of Sarajevo was in fact the first victim of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I know that he was one of the first victims that was killed. Whether it could be termed as a war or not is open, I think, to interpretation. To me, this was an innocent person killed at a wedding and I felt it shouldn't have anything to do with the events of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You believe that this had nothing to do with the events in the city, with the just-announced, published results of this referendum that was conducted without the participation of the Serbs. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It is my belief that the killing of the Serb at the wedding was used to justify the erection of the barricades of the city. That, and the result of the referendum, I believe, was exploited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs used the fact that a Serb was killed to erect barricades. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that as far as the Serbs were concerned this murder was like a message that in spite of their will and Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslims had expressed their desire for independence and had now started to commit murders? Isn't it possible for this to cause tension or concern in Yugoslavia, because immediately after the referendum they were being killed? Isn't that so, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would accept that the killing of the Serb might have been a message. However, I deem it I am probable that just because one Serb was killed the entire city of Sarajevo should be barricaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the monitoring mission of the European Community in Yugoslavia, I assume that you were familiar with the fact that a group of Muslims which attacked the wedding party was led by Ramiz Delalic, nicknamed Celo. He was a member of the Patriotic League, the party army of Alija Izetbegovic. Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have no knowledge as to who carried out the killing of the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Ramiz Delalic, Celo, who was a notorious criminal? And he had links with Alija Izetbegovic and the SDA leadership. Have you ever heard of this man?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Personally, I have not heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since Mr. Nice cited a document of yours, and that is a -- [In English] 1st and 2nd March, 1992. [Interpretation] The results of the referendum were announced. This is in tab 6 of the binder that I received. The referendum results were announced. Immediately after that there was the killing of a Serb. The Serbs were very, very much disturbed by this. So the sequence of events is without doubt as follows: The announcement of the referendum results and then the beginning of the attack on the Serbs, including this killing. And then you state in your report as follows: "[In English] Official SDS Demands: (a) All activities with regard to international recognition should be stopped." [Interpretation] So is it clear then that it was precisely these activities that began to cause conflicts, clashes, and murders, and that is the reason why the Serbs were making the demands they were making? Is that true, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It is my interpretation that what Radovan Karadzic had predicted to me that would happen if sovereignty was given to Bosnia was coming to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Radovan Karadzic envisaged that when the results of the referendum are published, Muslims would start killing Serbs, which is what happened. Is it perhaps Radovan Karadzic who organised the murder of this man Gardovic in the centre of Sarajevo, according to what you know, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: As I repeat, I have no idea who was responsible for the death of the Serb in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But let us look at the following points of this SDS demands. "[In English] Conference on BiH should be continued. Media should stop reporting as if BiH was already recognised." [Interpretation] Here you say: "[In English] The political situation, Ministry of Interior - not performing as it should be - 24 hours to settle on new composition. Assassins should be caught before the end of today." [Interpretation] And in brackets, "2 Muslims, 1 Croat." "[In English] They should be well-known criminals." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. The part that follows relates to the television, and it says it is spreading anti-Serb propaganda in such a way as for every party to have their own channel, meaning Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Is that so, Mr. Doyle? It is in your report.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. They are a copy of the demands that were given to me by the SDS Crisis Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This morning you were saying that the Minister of Information asked you to intervene with the Minister of the Police regarding his competencies regarding the media in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. The Minister of Information was keen to elicit my support in persuading the Minister of the Interior, that he, the Minister of Information should have more control of the national airwaves than he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, Mr. Doyle, as a man of great experience, a representative of the European Community in the area coming from a country with a democratic system, does it seem logical to you that the television be under the control of the Ministry of Police or the Ministry of Information?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't think it's appropriate for me to make comment on what are the internal workings of a country such as Bosnia. The fact that they may not conform with what we have in other countries of the European Community is, I believe, besides the point. I believe it was not appropriate for me to interfere in the internal workings of these two ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That may well be, but I just asked you whether you thought it logical for the Ministry of Police to be in control of television rather that the Ministry of Information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there is any significance in this point, we can make a decision about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My previous reference made to not the Ministry of Police but the Interior Ministry rather than the Ministry of Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's one and the same thing. Then you go on to speak -- you spoke earlier today about going to a press conference dealing with this referendum, and you were wearing civilian clothes because it was inappropriate for you to appear there in an official role, and you explained, when you were talking about it today, that Karadzic invited you to observe the Serbian referendum and you refused it, deeming it inappropriate. If that was inappropriate, to monitor the Serbian referendum, then why was it appropriate to attend the press conference of the other side? Didn't you find that inappropriate as well?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because the referendum was requested. The assistance of the European Union was requested by the referendum authorities. The European Union made the decision to send referendum observers, therefore I didn't think that it was in any way inappropriate that I be there. However, I felt for my own impartiality and to maintain that impartiality and so that my appearance in uniform might be exploited by the Serbs, I decided not to wear a uniform. So it was a personal decision based on my judgement of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Doyle. Is it indisputable, since that is something you said while explaining or justifying this remark with your military experience, that the barricades you saw in Sarajevo were erected hastily? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My opinion is that they all seemed to be erected at the same time, and they were very effective in cutting off the city, so it was my opinion that this had been planned in advance. I have no proof of that, but it is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you just said, and I noted it down, you said the barricades had been erected hastily, and that was something you concluded on the basis of your military experience. Therefore, after this event, the murder and the violence, the barricades were erected hastily. How do you connect that now with the remark, the observation that it was planned in advance and all the rest you had to say in this connection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness has said is that for such an operation - this was the effect of it - there must have been some planning in advance. It's you who are saying it was all hastily done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, no. It was the witness who said that, from what he could judge based on his military experience, he said in his examination-in-chief, that the barricades had been erected hastily. You must have that on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me find it. It's not my recollection that he talked about barricades being erected hastily, but let us clarify from the witness. Colonel, there are really two questions, one leading from the other. Did the barricades appear to be erected hastily, and if so, is that consistent with your view that there appeared to be some prior planning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is consistent. When I used the word "hastily," what I'm referring here to, Your Honour, is that in my opinion this was planned. Because the barricades went up hastily, it was my view that it was planned in advance. In other words, when I say "hastily," it meant they did not take too long for this plan to be put into action because I believe there was a plan there in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Doyle. Immediately below, you say there was shooting from the town on people, on the barricades, from the surrounding buildings. Who was it who shot at the men at the barricades?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have no idea, but it would be my opinion that they were not Serbs, because the Serbs were manning the barricades. So it was my presumption that they were either Croats or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And immediately after that, you met with Ejub Ganic at the Holiday Inn, and after that, with Karadzic. You met with both at the Holiday Inn on different floors, in different rooms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I distinctly remember meeting with Ejub Ganic. My notes refer to me meeting Karadzic. I don't personally recollect at this time remembering it was specifically him. I met with Ejub Ganic in the main lobby of the hotel. I cannot recall where I met with Radovan Karadzic, but I am almost certain it was he who handed me the demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Tell me, since you had met with both and they were at the same hotel, you met with both of them, what was the outcome of those meetings with them and your mediation effort? Was there a result with either party?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The result of the meeting with the SDS Crisis Committee with Radovan Karadzic was that I agreed I would pass on the demands of the committee to the Presidency, which I did by giving to Mr. Ganic. The result of my meeting with Mr. Ganic is that I got from him an agreement that there would be a requirement for the government of the Presidency to secure the safe return of the referendum observers to the airport. And it was in that context that I agreed that I would use myself in the convoy to go to the airport, which I duly did. I subsequently went down to one of the barricades, as is in my report, but I was not successful in persuading the Serbs to lift that barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that on the 3rd of March, Muslim barricades were erected.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
