utterances.text: And then Ganic and General Kukanjac appeared jointly on television, General Kukanjac being the then commander of the JNA in the area. And this joint appearance helped ease the tensions in the city and calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, since you are talking about the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia, you say you were concerned because troops were accumulating in Bosnia. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, did you have any information to the effect that the JNA withdrawing from Croatia was free to go to Bosnia, Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro, possibly, but there was no other area they could go to. Therefore, the troops from Croatia did not concentrate in Bosnia. They also went to Serbia and to other parts of the Yugoslavia as they were leaving Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the conditions of the agreement under which the JNA would withdraw from Croatia. In other words, I don't know if there was an agreement with the international community as to where that army would go. My one concern was that the because the Presidency did not look favourably on the JNA, a large build-up of those forces in Bosnia might not help the political situation, and therefore, I was concerned. I have no evidence as to where else they went to, but I would assume that they would have gone to places like Serbia, and Macedonia and Montenegro, but I don't know exactly where the balance of the military force went except to say that a large amount of their heavy weapons and their tanks went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you also state that a large part of JNA troops withdrawing from Croatia originally came from Bosnia. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why would then they have to go to Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: What I want to say here is that I don't know what percentage of the JNA army leaving Croatia, what percentage of those were Bosnians. I simply don't know. But we were aware that the element of the Croatian -- of the JNA army that was withdrawing from Croatia, a large amount of that that went to Bosnia subsequently became part of the Bosnian Serb army, and they were based primarily in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. I understood from your testimony in chief, and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. even noted it down somewhere, that you were satisfied that the JNA was really and honestly withdrawing from Bosnia at the time when it was topical.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I formed the opinion that after a lot of the JNA force that was Bosnian that consisted of Serbs when they went to Pale, that the balance of the federal army that were not from Bosnia but were stationed in Bosnia were anxious to leave the country and return to Serbia. Yes, I would agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. You say that when you arrived, the situation was very tense. The only flights from the airport were intended to evacuate families of JNA members and JNA troops leaving Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But then you go on to say that you cannot judge about the situation in the city because you did not move around the city. All information you had was secondhand about activities in the centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, not particularly, because at this time I had quite a lot of contact with General Kukanjac and General Aksentijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do say that the JNA did not interfere in these clashes. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Up to the time that I was there, and I would have to refer to my notes to get a date, but at the start of the fighting in the city of Sarajevo, it was my belief that the JNA were not anxious to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. But I suppose it is a fact that you could have established as a monitor. You talked about a meeting you had with the Serb leadership Ilidza. Prior to that Bell from the BBC told you that there were about 2.500 refugees from Zvornik and you related that immediately to Karadzic, and Karadzic responded that he didn't believe that. Was that so?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you make any effort to establish the truth?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: As I said, it was difficult for me to establish the truth, because at that stage the sources of information that I would have used would have come from the European Community Monitor mission, and as I mentioned it earlier, it was getting more difficult for them to move into areas where we wished to find out what the situation was because the JNA informed them they could not give them freedom of movement or safety and security. So I was relying on secondhand information to find out what the situation was. I did not have an independent source to verify what the situation was in these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you also mentioned that from what you could see at the hotel, the non-Serb personnel had left and seeking an answer to why they left, you established that they had in fact fled because they did not feel safe any more. Was that the reason?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, that was not the reason. They left because they were forced to leave. It wasn't their choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I understood you as saying that they had left for security reasons. Are you now saying that somebody had expelled them?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was when I asked the question of the Serb new community leadership at Ilidza why it was that these people were moved, it was they who said they were moved for their own safety. It was not the Muslims themselves who said that. We took this as being a forced removal of an element of the population of Sarajevo, and it was not something they would have chosen themselves in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the Serbs told you they had expelled Muslims from Ilidza. Is that what you're saying? And they had told you themselves that they had left because they didn't feel safe, and you interpreted that as an expelling of the Muslims, and that was the information you got from the local Serbs, from the leadership at Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was not the Serbs who told me they expelled the Muslims. It was the Serbs who told me that they had moved the Muslims to the centre of the city for their own safety. It was not the Serbs that said they were expelled. It was others who told me that this amounted to an -- I want to get proper wording here. These people, in my view, the Muslims, did not request to be moved to the centre of the city. They had no choice in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But those local Serbs from Ilidza, whom you call local Serb, they invited you to dinner, didn't they? You spoke about that. And you concluded that they wanted to abuse --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear a part of this sentence. To abuse it how?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: First of all, I should say that it was my opinion that the reason why I was invited to dinner was that I would be on the side of this new Serb community. It was only when the representative of the Serbs who spoke at the dinner said that they had moved the Muslims for their own safety that I realised that this might not be the case and that I might -- my position might be exploited. I mentioned this in a reply to the speech, and as a consequence of that, I decided to leave the dinner, and this I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then after that, if I understood you correctly, at this Bosna Hotel, you reached that agreement, the cease-fire agreement with Karadzic. Is that correct? Is the timing I mention correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would have to check in my notes as to the specific dates of this, but in the negotiations with Radovan Karadzic around that time, they were conducted at that hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is in fact the agreement you reached with him at that time, and that is the agreement that was concluded a few days later, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I think that may be the case, but I would need some time to refer to my notes on it. I can't -- I can't ascertain the date of that dinner that I was invited to, but I can confirm the date that we had negotiated with Radovan Karadzic on the cease-fire. So I can't marry both of them up together at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't have to marry both of them up. At any rate, you reached an agreement with Karadzic on a cease-fire, and later on precisely this agreement that you reached with him was -- became the agreement that all three sides -- that all three sides signed, and that's the one that we already discussed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Cutileiro said after that that all three sides were against the use of force with a view to taking any kind of territories and also in favour of the return of refugees; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, you said that somebody had threatened the television station, the television station would be targeted within the next half hour. You reacted immediately, you talked to Karadzic, he guaranteed that this would not happen, but nevertheless some shells fell. That's what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: So it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it clear to you on the basis of that that these were things that were out of control, out of their control, and that perhaps somebody who got furious because of the statements he heard and the lies he heard did this and that this was not under Radovan Karadzic's control, and on the basis of what you've been saying, he wasn't even in Pale at the time, because this is the first time I ever hear about this, from you.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is that on the 18th of April when the telephone allegedly from Pale came to Sarajevo Television and they sent it on to me and I got in contact with Radovan Karadzic through his aide, it was Radovan Karadzic who said, "Do not worry, the PT -- the television station will not be targeted." I can only assume then that he would have had influence in deciding whether it would be targeted or not. Had I not known that -- had I known that Radovan Karadzic allegedly was not in control, I probably wouldn't have gone to him to get an agreement or to get an assurance that the television station would not be targeted. But because I felt that he was in control, and the fact that he acknowledged to me that this attack would not take place, led me further to believe that he did have influence in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I assume that those days when you were in Sarajevo there was chaos reigning there. Does it seem probable to you that Radovan Karadzic could have had control over just about anyone who could have fired a shell? Weren't there elements of anarchy, a lack of discipline there? You're an experienced soldier; you should know that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: In my discussions with Radovan Karadzic, he certainly gave me the belief that he controlled everything in relation to the Serbs and the Bosnian Serb army at that stage. I have no reason to disbelieve that. In a state of conflict of this nature, of course there is the chance that renegades here and there may act independently, but it is my belief that part of political leadership is responsibility for those who are under your control or under your influence, and it is my belief that Radovan Karadzic had that. I can't prove that he controlled every Serb in Sarajevo or the outlying area of Pale, but I assume that he could, and I expected that he could because he deemed himself to be the leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, but when he told you that no one would attack and this happened nevertheless, wasn't that a sign to you that there were things that were not under his control? He would not have given you his word and then had something like that happen if he could have prevented this from happening. Was it your impression that he was deceiving you or that he was speaking to you frankly?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would accept that he was speaking to me frankly, and I would acknowledge that. Maybe he didn't have control in that particular instant. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's not dwell on that any longer now. You spoke about Foca and ethnic cleansing. You were not directly involved in the events concerned, but some of your monitors had gone to Foca. It was my understanding that that is what you were saying. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: What I was saying that some of the monitors of the mission were attempting to get to Foca, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was my understanding that en route they were warned by members of the JNA that they could not guarantee their safety because they did not have things in Foca under their own control. A few minutes before that, you were saying that the JNA was not interfering in any conflict. Was this a well-intentioned suggestion made by the members of the JNA, that they did not know what was going on and they could not guarantee their security, or do you think that they stopped them on purpose so that they would conceal what was going on in Foca? What did you infer on that basis, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I did not say that the JNA were not interfering in any conflict. What I did say was that as far as I could ascertain in the city of Sarajevo, they were not interfering, which is distinctly different from what might have been happening elsewhere in the country. I have no detailed knowledge as to what was happening in these areas, but I do know that it was the JNA who advised the monitor mission that they could not in their own safety get to a location like Foca. That being the case, it would be, in my view, unusual that the military army that was in present -- was in so many numbers in this republic could not guarantee the safety of a few monitors, because they were well spread out. So I simply don't know why the JNA did not allow them to go to Foca. It was remarked by the JNA to the team that they, the JNA, could not guarantee their safety. One has to ask the question why they wouldn't guarantee their safety. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they give an answer? Did they give any answer? I assume that they asked them, "Why can you not guarantee our safety?" There were units there, weren't there? They warned them then; right? And then you say further on that Koljevic offered to help. However, later on this was not carried through, but everybody was all worked up about it. Did Koljevic seem sincere to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have no reason to believe that he wasn't sincere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And immediately after that, you say that in the Hotel Bosna in Ilidza -- so this was the area where Serbs lived, and as a matter of fact, you described that the Muslims had left the area or were expelled or I don't know what and that the first fighting took place on the 22nd of April at 5.00 a.m. and that this was an attack launched by the Muslims. Isn't at that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm assuming it was attacked by non-Serbs. Exactly who, I simply don't know, but the people who were defending the location were the Serbs, so I presume it was either Muslims or Croats. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you could have assessed that this was a fierce attack because you say that there were 13 casualties.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: What I saw that day was approximately 40 to 50 Serb paramilitaries, heavily armed, and they were returning fire to a location from which fire was being directed at them. It was later in the afternoon when a television crew went out and carried out some interviews, some of the members of the Serb -- the Serb paramilitaries, that they were told that there were 13 people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at the beginning, Gardovic was killed, and that was beginning, in the centre of Sarajevo. Then there was this attack by the Muslims on this Serb settlement in Ilidza, 13 persons killed. And is it clear to you, Mr. Doyle, as a monitor, that conflicts were being caused precisely by the Muslim side? And add to that the fact that Karadzic was the first one to sign the cease-fire agreement and that they had an agreement with Cutileiro. He had a compromise with Cengic, that all of this was rejected. And then when you put all the pieces together, can't it be seen that it was the Muslim side that behaved most aggressively in all these events that took place after the partial referendum? Is that picture clear to you or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, that picture is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, on the 22nd of April, 13 people were killed in a Serb settlement, and they were killed by the attacking forces. And on the 23rd of April, Karadzic was the first one to accept the cease-fire agreement and sign it. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's what I said, but I think it is you who is inferring that all of this was to be blamed on the Muslims and the Serbs were the sufferers. I don't accept that in the context of the overall picture I had of Sarajevo and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not being contested that Izetbegovic and his people played the role of victim successfully, but these are facts that you testified about, Mr. Doyle. Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's just pure comment by you. Now, if you've got questions, you must ask them, not comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I'm not going to -- I'm not going to make any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 28th of April, you were persuading Izetbegovic to go to Lisbon, and then the air traffic control from Belgrade did not give approval for the plane to land. Do you know what the reason was for that? Did you get any kind of explanation? And the following morning it could leave. You say that the plane left the following morning at 10.00 a.m. So in the evening they did not give this approval, and in the morning they did. What's the point of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't think I'm making a point, I'm just stating a fact. When the plane was not allowed to land in Sarajevo, I passed that message on to Ambassador Cutileiro in Lisbon, and he said he would try and persuade the authorities, I presume in Belgrade, to allow this aircraft to land the following day, and I assume he was successful. But I'm simply saying that the plane was not allowed to land in Sarajevo. I had the president there under UN escort, and my objective then was to try and get the president safely back to the Presidency. What happened between the evening when the plane was not allowed to land and the following morning when it was allowed to land, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I assume that you did not infer that somebody from Belgrade was impeding the possibility of going to the peace conference, because what did not happen in the evening did happen in the morning.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You gave some comments, and it's here in one of the tabs, the letter of the mayor of Sarajevo, and you yourself said that it was an exaggeration. Isn't that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: What I would say about that is that in lots of reports that I got from all sides there was the general tendency to exaggerate, and this, in my view, was one of those. I do not in any way dispute the fact that the situation was getting pretty desperate and that there was an urgent need for corridors to be open to get humanitarian aid into the city, but from the experience I had in the former Yugoslavia over the 12 months, I would say that all sides from time to time, in my opinion, seemed to exaggerate the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I don't know how much more time I will have, Mr. May, I would like, before that, for us to have a look at this report that you sent from the talks you had with me. Mr. Nice apologised for quoting extensively. However, his quotations were rather distorted, I should say. Since I have your report here - it's your very own text - I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 12. And I don't accept for a moment that Mr. Nice distorted what was said. We can read it for ourselves. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have your text. I haven't got a text of my own. So you say that the talks took place in accordance with the instructions you received from Lord Carrington and Ambassador Cutileiro. That's what's written here. Isn't that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say, since I want to go through all these details, I want this to be fair.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm going to draw your attention to the places where I think the distortion was particularly pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "[In English] Having clearly defined my role and the nature of my mission, I called for Belgrade support in --" [Interpretation] then you say: "[In English] maintaining the present cease-fire in BiH." [Interpretation] So you sought the support of Belgrade so that Belgrade would help maintain the cease-fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. This would be by using its influence in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you say: "[In English] Reopening the airport at Sarajevo and guaranteeing the unhindered passage of humanitarian relief supplies." [Interpretation] So you asked for our support in that as well, that we support the maintenance of the cease-fire, unhindered passage of humanitarian relief supplies. "[In English] Around the city: Halting the expulsions of non-Serbs from occupied settlements and allowing those who so wished to return to them." [Interpretation] This is where you sought the support of Belgrade. Isn't that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. These were the -- these were the points that I was requested to bring up at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yes. That's where you sought the support of Belgrade. And for all of that you did receive the support of Belgrade. You say in the following paragraph: "[In English] I stressed that Lord Carrington was anxious for Milosevic to use his influence." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth, to use his influence to a maximum. And I say to you, after having listened to you carefully, and that's what you said yourself: "[In English]... he believed -- he believed Lord Carrington was aware that Belgrade was doing its best to support the peace process in Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Secondly: "[In English] In all communications with the Bosnian Serbs Belgrade pressed for them to avoid bloodshed. Sarajevo was the key problem position, and if the city could be pacified, solutions would usually be easier elsewhere in the republic. Belgrade shared the objectives of reopening Sarajevo airport, putting the city Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. under UN control and removing the artillery from the mountains. This had been made clear publicly on repeated occasions." [Interpretation] Are you aware, Mr. Doyle, that all of these positions of mine were presented in public as well? And then I say to you: "[In English] It was now the turn of the UN to take action accordingly. Milosevic expressed keen interest in knowing when the airport might be reopened and when Lord Carrington might visit Sarajevo." [Interpretation] As you remember, I thought that a visit by Lord Carrington to Sarajevo would give an additional impetus to the conference that was supposed to achieve peace in Bosnia. Isn't that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The points that I'm raising here are, in my opinion, an accurate reflection of what was mentioned at the meeting that I had with you, and I was repeating what you said that Lord Carrington believed to be the case. So I'm simply reflecting what you've said to me, and I'm reflecting that as accurately as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. And then you say that I supported the proposal, strongly endorsed the proposal of Radovan Karadzic, to be quite precise. This is your report: "[In English] Milosevic strongly endorsed the proposal from the Bosnian Serb leader Karadzic that UN observers be attached -- to be attached to each unit of the Bosnian Serb forces in order to witness the facts on the ground." [Interpretation] Wasn't that a logical and sincere offer made by Karadzic? And I believed that you would support it too, to provide observers so that they could truly bear witness to what was going on rather than having the Bosnian Serbs blamed for everything that was going on. As you said here, you're going to be blamed for that shell regardless of whether you fired it or not. So wasn't this a very frank proposal made by Karadzic to provide observers and each and every one of their units so you could see that they had nothing to hide? And further on, you say that: "[In English] Belgrade was constantly cast in the role of aggressor, but there was not a single Serb from Serbia fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If the contrary were true, it would be impossible to keep secret." [Interpretation] And then I mention to you there let's try to keep this as short as possible, that our police already "[In English]... arrested 1.300 people who had been in the area carrying weapons for which they had no licence." [Interpretation] And then you say that I insisted to evacuate cadets, as you put it here, from the Marsal Tito barracks, even at the cost of leaving behind heavy weapons, because I did not think that a single soldier should be killed for the sake of keeping some weapons there, even though others or anybody could have opposed this. I really cared about preserving the lives of these young people who came to do their military service in the JNA, not to get killed out there. And then paragraph 3, you say: "[In English] Milosevic pointed out more than once that Belgrade had vigorously condemned the shelling of Sarajevo, which had been a futile and criminal exercise for which the perpetrators should be punished." [Interpretation] And so on. And then I move on to say: "[In English] Milosevic stated that Belgrade could not halt its supply of humanitarian aid to Bosnian Serbs." [Interpretation] Of course not. Of course not. How we could leave the people out there in that kind of situation? Helpless people. You say here in parentheses: "Clothing, food," and I said yes, we are giving them material assistance, we are giving them food, goods, everything. "[In English] But also complained that there had been no coverage by the Western media --" [Interpretation] This was a misquote by Mr. Nice. He said that the Westerners did not take part in this. "[In English]... there had been no coverage by the Western media of two Serbian relief convoys which had distributed food and medical goods impartially to the three ethnic communities in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] By then we had already sent two convoys to Sarajevo to get in and to give all citizens aid by way of food and medicines on a non-discriminatory basis. And then you move on to say: "He agreed --" I mean I agreed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're coming to the end. Do you know anything about these convoys, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with the convoys. I would just like to state here that I have no argument with Mr. Milosevic in the content of this meeting we had. It was Mr. Milosevic who said all these things and I was simply there to accurately reflect what he believed to be the case and what he said was the case. I don't know what the reality was, but I felt it was very important that whatever Mr. Milosevic would say to me, that I would accurately reflect that back to Lord Carrington, and this is what I did the best way I could. That was one of the reasons why I asked if I could have somebody to take notes so that I would not make any mistake. So I agree with what Mr. Milosevic is saying. How accurate it is in practice I have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now time to adjourn. Mr. Milosevic, dealing with the time available to you, we have in mind that this witness's statement was admitted partially under Rule 92 bis and therefore you should have extra time to reflect that. We also bear in mind that this is an important witness in nature of his role. In those circumstances, we've decided that you should have a total of three hours cross-examination. That leaves you one hour and five minutes tomorrow. Do the amicus anticipate any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I would have about 15 or 20 minutes for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be as well if we could finish by the adjournment. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning, please, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of August, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
